news.title: Biden Reveals What Prompted His 'Terrible Night' During Trump Debate
news.text: Former President Joe Biden has revealed the personal turmoil behind his disastrous June 2024 presidential debate against Donald Trump, writing that the emotional toll of his son Hunter's criminal convictions weighed heavily on him as he took to the stage. In his newly released memoir, Promise Me, America, Biden reflects on the Atlanta debate, describing it as "a terrible night" that triggered a political crisis from which his reelection campaign would not recover. While acknowledging that he appeared tired, struggled to articulate his answers and lost his train of thought during the televised showdown, Biden pushes back against the suggestion that his performance reflected cognitive decline. Instead, he points to a combination of physical exhaustion, illness and personal anguish, particularly the conviction of his son Hunter on federal gun charges just 16 days earlier. The debate, held on June 27, 2024, marked a turning point in Biden's presidency. Within 24 days, mounting pressure from Democrats would force him to abandon his bid for a second term and endorse Vice President Kamala Harris. Hunter Biden's Conviction Was Weighing on Him Biden writes that his son's legal troubles were never far from his mind in the weeks leading up to the debate. On June 11, 2024, Hunter Biden was found guilty by a Delaware jury on three federal felony counts relating to his purchase of a firearm in 2018 while struggling with crack cocaine addiction. The conviction came after years of federal investigations and intense political scrutiny, which Biden says took a significant emotional toll on their family. "On June 11, my son Hunter had been convicted of three felonies in a federal courtroom in Wilmington, Delaware. And it was breaking my heart," Biden writes. "Even more than that, I lived daily with the fear — and the guilt — that it was going to break Hunter." Biden recounts how Hunter's struggles with substance abuse intensified following the 2015 death of his older brother, Beau Biden, from brain cancer. Despite Hunter's efforts to maintain sobriety, his legal problems continued to dominate headlines, with Republicans frequently using the investigations as a political issue during Biden's presidency. "In the end, they failed to break Hunter," Biden writes. "But I would be lying if I didn't admit they took a piece out of me." The former president says he believed his son was being subjected to unusually aggressive treatment because of his political connections. "Would anyone have been through what Hunter endured if they weren't my son? Almost definitely not," he writes. "It was obvious. Hunter was being raked over the coals because of me." Biden argues that Republicans were using the investigations to damage his presidency, but says his greatest concern was the effect on his son. Biden's Belief That Hunter Was Politically Targeted Hunter Biden faced two separate federal prosecutions brought by special counsel David Weiss. The first resulted in his June 2024 gun conviction. Prosecutors argued that Hunter had lied on a federal firearms application by denying unlawful drug use or addiction when purchasing a Colt Cobra .38-caliber revolver in October 2018. He was also convicted of illegally possessing the firearm. A separate federal tax case in California involved nine charges alleging that Hunter had failed to pay at least $1.4 million in taxes between 2016 and 2019. In September 2024, Hunter unexpectedly pleaded guilty to all nine counts, avoiding a trial. In Promise Me, America, Biden argues that the prosecutions were politically motivated and that his son was treated differently because of his family name. He points out that Hunter had repaid the outstanding taxes, interest and penalties, questioning whether someone without his political connections would have faced the same level of scrutiny. In December 2024, Biden issued his son a full and unconditional pardon covering federal offenses committed or potentially committed between January 1, 2014, and December 1, 2024. The decision reversed Biden's earlier public pledges not to intervene in the cases and prompted criticism from Republicans, who accused him of using presidential power to protect his family. What Happened During the Trump Debate? By the time Biden arrived at the CNN studios in Atlanta on June 27, he was already physically depleted. He had recently completed an intensive international travel schedule, including trips to France and Italy, and was still feeling unwell. Although he tested negative for COVID-19, Biden appeared raspy and struggled to deliver several answers during the debate. His performance was particularly difficult when discussing healthcare and his administration's efforts to lower prescription drug costs. At one point, while attempting to highlight his achievements on healthcare, he delivered a confused response that ended with the words: "We finally beat Medicare." Trump repeatedly attacked Biden over his age, his administration's record and his ability to serve another four years. Biden acknowledges in the memoir that the debate was a major setback. "What should have been a highlight of the debate became Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job," he writes. Walking off the stage alongside former First Lady Jill Biden, he was under no illusion that the evening had gone well. When Jill asked how he was feeling, Biden recalls replying: "Well, I screwed that up." He adds that his actual response at the time was considerably more colorful. Biden Thought He Would Get a Chance to Redeem Himself Despite the poor performance, Biden says he initially believed he could recover. He points in his memoir to previous presidential candidates, including Ronald Reagan and Barack Obama, who had struggled during early debates but were given opportunities to improve in subsequent encounters. Biden argues that his situation was different because the political reaction to his performance quickly became a debate about whether he should remain in the race at all. "The difference in 2024 was not that I had a bad debate," he writes. "The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me." The former president describes the media coverage that followed as "one of the worst poundings ever delivered by the free press." Democratic lawmakers, donors and party strategists began questioning whether he could defeat Trump in November, with calls for him to withdraw growing louder by the day. Biden insists he was fully aware of the mounting pressure. "I followed it. Hell, I was living it," he writes. "I knew exactly how many Democratic members of Congress and governors had pulled their support of me." Pelosi and Schumer Turned Up the Pressure Biden also offers a candid account of the private conversations with senior Democrats that ultimately contributed to his decision to leave the race. He expresses particular frustration with former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, whom he accuses of publicly presenting the decision as his alone while privately working to persuade elected officials and delegates to abandon his candidacy. Biden recalls that Pelosi challenged polling presented by his senior adviser Mike Donilon, telling him bluntly that there were no polls showing a path to victory. The former president says the episode left him feeling betrayed by a longtime political ally, although he notes that the pair later repaired their relationship over an Italian lunch without revisiting the summer's events. He also recounts a difficult meeting with then-Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer at his beach house in Rehoboth, Delaware. According to Biden, Schumer warned that he could no longer win and risked being left with only "five Democratic senators still supporting me." Biden recalls telling Schumer he had "a lot of gumption" coming to his home to urge him to abandon the campaign. The conversations illustrate how quickly support within the Democratic Party unraveled following the Atlanta debate. Biden's Decision to Drop Out of the 2024 Race Biden maintains that he believed the election remained winnable, but ultimately concluded that continuing his campaign against the wishes of senior Democratic leaders risked damaging the party's chances in November. On the night of July 20, he drafted a letter announcing his withdrawal from the presidential race. "Believe it or not, I slept well that night," he writes. The following afternoon, July 21, Biden formally announced that he was stepping aside and endorsed Harris as the Democratic nominee. His decision dramatically reshaped the 2024 election, setting up a contest between Harris and Trump that ultimately ended with the Republican's return to the White House. Promise Me, America, published by Little, Brown and Company, is out today. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Joe Biden has revealed the personal turmoil behind his disastrous June 2024 presidential debate against Donald Trump,.
news.author: Hannah Parry

news.title: Conservative influencer Brett Cooper admits she has left MAGA: ‘There was a lot of gaslighting that took place’
news.text:
Conservative influencer Brett Cooper has left MAGA, admitting that “there was a lot of gaslighting” in President Donald Trump’s base. 

In October 2024, weeks before Trump would go on to defeat then-Vice President Kamala Harris for a second term in the White House, Cooper was all smiles in a photo she posted to Instagram, wearing a MAGA hat on horseback. She captioned the photo, “Sry Kamala, this is what joy looks like.”

Two years later, Cooper is disheartened with the movement she so fiercely backed. 

“I’m not part of [MAGA] any more,” Cooper, a 25-year-old with 1.7 million YouTube subscribers, told the Financial Times in a new interview. “I think I’ve moved on.”

Cooper’s rift from the MAGA movement started with the Trump administration’s handling of files related to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein last year. 

Trump begrudgingly signed a bill to release the files after months of resistance, with critics not only questioning the transparency of the administration, but also whether a more sinister cover-up was taking place. The president, who ran in the same social circles as Epstein decades ago, has denied claims of a cover-up, telling reporters, “I have nothing to hide.”

Cooper remembered seeing a social media post from Trump suggesting that those still demanding answers about Epstein’s crimes and associates were no longer part of MAGA. 

“Ok, well, I guess I’m not!” she recalled thinking. 

She, like other Republicans, also took issue with Trump starting a war in Iran more than eight months ago that caused gas prices to soar — after the president promised no more prolonged military conflicts. She also didn’t like the administration’s response to economic concerns, as many Americans struggled with stubborn inflation.

“There was a lot of gaslighting that took place,” Cooper said. “It’s just been so belittling.”

Cooper, a former Daily Wire host, now focuses her conservative values on more cultural and entertainment videos rather than politically heavy episodes for her podcast, The Brett Cooper Show. 

Despite her dissatisfaction with the Trump administration, she still voted Republican in the midterm elections, where Democrats took control of the House and the Senate. Trump has dodged blame for the massive losses. 

“It’s just kind of closing the chapter,” she said. “We’re excited to see what’s next.”

Podcaster Joe Rogan, who endorsed Trump in the 2024 election, admitted after the GOP midterm shellacking, “They didn’t just lose the podcast bros. They lost most of the country.”

Rogan and other podcasters helped Trump to victory in 2024, but nearly halfway through his term, they are showing some buyer’s remorse. 

Since Trump returned to the Oval Office, Rogan has criticized the Iran war, the president’s massive immigration crackdown and the administration’s handling of the Epstein files. 

“When you get into a war that no one wants to be in, when you got militarized police in the streets wearing masks and no ID,” Rogan said while reflecting on Republicans’ election losses.
news.summary: Cooper listed reasons why she left the movement, including President Trump’s handling of the Epstein files
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

news.title: Biden's New Memoir Mentions Donald Trump Nearly 200 Times
news.text: Former President Joe Biden's newly released memoir, Promise Me, America, reveals just how much Donald Trump loomed over his presidency, with the Republican mentioned nearly 200 times throughout the book. From the 2020 election and the January 6 Capitol attack to NATO, the economy and Trump's return to office in 2025, Biden repeatedly revisits his predecessor, contrasting his own policies and approach to the presidency with those of the man he defeated in 2020, only to be succeeded by four years later. Much of the memoir is sharply critical of Trump's leadership, rhetoric and conduct, particularly his efforts to overturn the 2020 election result and his response to the Capitol attack. The frequency of the references underlines how central Trump remains to Biden's account of his time in the White House, even after leaving office. Biden also reveals a more complicated relationship behind their public clashes. He recalls unexpectedly warm private encounters, including a handwritten letter Trump left on the Resolute Desk on Inauguration Day in 2021 and a surprisingly friendly Oval Office meeting following Trump's 2024 election victory. Promise Me, America, published by Little, Brown and Company, is out today. Newsweek has reached out to the White House for comment. Trump's Inauguration Day Letter Surprised Biden One of the more unexpected revelations in the memoir concerns the private letter Trump left for Biden before departing the White House on January 20, 2021. Trump refused to attend Biden's inauguration, becoming the first outgoing president since Andrew Johnson in 1869 to skip his successor's swearing-in ceremony. However, he maintained one longstanding presidential tradition by leaving a note on the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. Addressed simply "To '46'" in heavy Sharpie ink, the two-page handwritten letter struck an unexpectedly gracious tone. According to the text reproduced in Biden's memoir, Trump described working in the Oval Office as "a blessing beyond imagination" and expressed confidence that Biden would not simply be swept along by history, writing that he knew how much the incoming president loved the American people. He concluded by offering a blessing to Biden and his wife, Jill. Biden describes the letter as "beguiling," particularly because of the contrast between Trump's frequently hostile public comments and the warmth of his private message. The former president writes that the note read almost as though it had come from "an old friend." January 6 and Trump's Role in the Capitol Attack In contrast, one of the most forceful passages in the memoir is Biden's reflections on the January 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. Biden recalls watching the violence unfold on television from his home in Wilmington, Delaware, as supporters of Trump stormed the Capitol in an effort to disrupt the certification of the 2020 election results. He argues that Trump's refusal to accept his defeat, despite numerous unsuccessful legal challenges, represented a fundamental breach of American democratic traditions. Biden is particularly critical of Trump's response as the attack unfolded, accusing him of watching the violence for hours without acting decisively to stop it. Describing the events as a "dereliction of duty," Biden writes that Trump was "leading an insurrection." The former president says the attack fundamentally changed his understanding of the presidency he was about to inherit. Rather than viewing his administration as beginning with his January 20 inauguration, Biden writes that, in many ways, his presidency began on January 6, when the immediate challenge became protecting democratic institutions. He also revisits Trump's post-election pressure campaign in Georgia, including his effort to persuade Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to find 11,780 additional votes. Biden presents the episode as further evidence of Trump's willingness to challenge established democratic processes to remain in power. The 2020 Election Campaign and Biden's Decision to Run In his memoir, Biden traces his decision to challenge Trump in 2020 to the 2017 white supremacist rally in Charlottesville, Virginia. The former president recalls being deeply disturbed by Trump's response to the violence, particularly his comments about there being "very fine people on both sides." For Biden, the episode reinforces his belief that the country was facing a fundamental test of its political values. He describes the presidential campaign as a "battle for the soul of the nation," presenting his candidacy as an effort to restore civility and democratic norms to American politics. Throughout the memoir, Biden contrasts his political philosophy with Trump's approach, arguing that the former president encouraged division and hostility rather than attempting to unite the country. The 2020 campaign ultimately became one of the defining personal and political rivalries of Biden's career, with the two men continuing to clash long after the election was decided. COVID-19 and Criticism of Trump's Pandemic Response Biden devotes considerable attention to Trump's handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, although he acknowledges one significant achievement of the previous administration. He credits Operation Warp Speed, launched under Trump, with accelerating the development of coronavirus vaccines and helping make vaccines available in record time. However, Biden argues that the administration failed to establish an effective federal distribution strategy before leaving office. He also criticizes Trump's treatment of public health officials, including Dr. Anthony Fauci, and his promotion of unproven treatments during the pandemic. Biden recalls the September 2020 presidential debate, during which Trump repeatedly clashed with him over the pandemic response. Trump tested positive for COVID-19 days later, an episode Biden references while criticizing the former president's approach to testing and masking protocols. Foreign Policy, NATO and Relations With World Leaders Trump's foreign policy record is another recurring subject in the memoir. Biden portrays his administration as attempting to repair relationships with America's traditional allies after four years of strained diplomatic ties under Trump. He recalls entering office determined to reassure international partners that "America's back," following the previous administration's withdrawals from international agreements, including the Paris Climate Agreement, the Iran nuclear deal and the Open Skies Treaty. The memoir also includes accounts of private conversations with foreign leaders who had dealt directly with Trump. Biden recalls former German Chancellor Angela Merkel describing Trump as "emotional" and suggesting that his international approach was driven by "mood swings rather than facts." He also references Merkel's apparent confusion over Trump's relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Biden draws comparisons between Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, suggesting that Netanyahu displayed "Trump-like tendencies" through his challenges to judicial institutions and efforts to maintain political power. The former president uses these examples to argue that Trump's approach to international relations weakened confidence in American leadership and encouraged instability among Western allies. Afghanistan Withdrawal and the Deal Biden Inherited From Trump The chaotic U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in August 2021 receives considerable attention in the memoir, with Biden defending his decision to end America's longest war while pointing to the constraints created by Trump's administration. Biden places particular emphasis on the February 2020 Doha Agreement, negotiated between the Trump administration and the Taliban. The agreement established a May 1, 2021, deadline for the withdrawal of American forces and included provisions for the release of 5,000 Taliban prisoners. Biden describes the arrangement as a "ticking time bomb," arguing that it left his administration with limited options. He writes that failing to meet the withdrawal deadline would likely have triggered renewed Taliban attacks against the approximately 2,500 American troops remaining in Afghanistan, potentially forcing the United States to send thousands more service members into the country. Although Biden accepts ultimate responsibility for the execution of the withdrawal, he maintains that the agreement negotiated by Trump significantly restricted his choices. Trump's Economic Policies and Biden's 'Middle-Out' Approach Biden's memoir often contrasts his economic agenda with the policies pursued during Trump's first presidency. Drawing on his childhood in Scranton, Pennsylvania, Biden argues that economic growth should benefit working families rather than disproportionately rewarding wealthy individuals and corporations. He criticizes Trump's 2017 tax legislation and the broader Republican philosophy of supply-side economics, describing the approach as a "silk stocking screw" that benefited those already at the top. In contrast, Biden points to legislation passed during his presidency, including the American Rescue Plan and the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, as evidence that government investment can produce tangible benefits for ordinary Americans. He also takes aim at the Trump administration's repeated promises to prioritize infrastructure spending, recalling the much-discussed "Infrastructure Week" that failed to produce the sweeping legislative results Trump had promised. Biden argues that rebuilding the economy "from the middle out and the bottom up" was essential to demonstrating that democracy could deliver meaningful improvements to people's lives. Biden Recalls Trump's Unexpected Praise in 2024 Oval Office Meeting One of the most surprising passages in the memoir concerns a meeting between Biden and Trump on November 13, 2024, shortly after Trump's election victory. The meeting marked the beginning of the presidential transition and was intended to demonstrate a peaceful transfer of power following another bitter election campaign. Biden writes that Trump surprised him by adopting a remarkably friendly tone. "He was so friendly that I thought he might be putting me on," Biden recalls, describing the interaction as bordering on fawning. According to Biden, Trump praised his administration's record on job creation, describing it as "extraordinary." Trump also reportedly suggested that, if politics were not involved, the two men might be "good friends." However, Biden says the conversation also revealed differences in how the two men approached international affairs. The 2024 Debate and Biden's Decision to Leave the Presidential Race The memoir also examines the events that ultimately ended Biden's campaign for a second term. Biden reveals that he initially questioned whether debating Trump in June 2024 was necessary, but eventually agreed to participate in the televised Atlanta debate. His performance became a defining moment of the campaign, with concerns about his age and ability to serve another four years quickly overshadowing discussions of his administration's legislative record. The aftermath brought mounting pressure from Democratic lawmakers, donors and allies, including Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, for Biden to reconsider his candidacy. He ultimately stepped aside in July 2024, endorsing Vice President Kamala Harris as his replacement. Trump's Second Term and the January 6 Pardons Biden's criticism of Trump continues beyond the 2024 election and into the opening weeks of the Republican's second presidency. One of his strongest objections concerns Trump's decision to issue pardons and commutations to defendants charged or convicted in connection with the January 6 Capitol attack. Biden criticizes the sweeping clemency granted to more than 1,500 January 6 defendants, arguing that it undermined accountability for the violence at the Capitol. Reflecting on Trump's role in the events of January 6, Biden writes that what Trump did that day "should follow him to his grave." He also describes Trump's early executive orders and policy decisions in 2025 as confirmation of his concerns about the direction of the country. Biden characterizes Trump's return to office as the beginning of a "crueler government" that sought to tear down institutions and inflame existing divisions. He further criticizes what he saw as Trump's unwillingness to build on the accomplishments of previous administrations, writing that the president "seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else's accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down." The memoir's closing reflections suggest that Biden views Trump's second presidency not as a departure from his first, but as an extension of the political approach that defined their rivalry. Ukraine, Congressional Republicans and Trump's Influence Biden also discusses Trump's influence over congressional Republicans and its implications for American support of Ukraine. He recalls difficulties securing continued military assistance for Kyiv as Republican opposition in the House became increasingly influenced by Trump's "America First" political philosophy. Biden points to House Republicans' reluctance to challenge MAGA-aligned members and references the reaction to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's address to Congress, when some lawmakers refused to applaud. He presents the political divisions as a significant obstacle to maintaining bipartisan support for Ukraine as it defended itself against Russia's invasion. The discussion reflects Biden's broader concern that Trump's political influence extended beyond his own administration, shaping Republican foreign policy positions even while Biden was president. Nuclear Weapons and the New START Treaty Another foreign policy issue Biden raises is the future of the New START nuclear arms control treaty between the United States and Russia. The agreement, which limited the two countries' deployed strategic nuclear weapons, was approaching its expiration in February 2021, just weeks after Biden took office. Biden criticizes the Trump administration for "not lifting a finger" to extend the agreement before leaving office. He says one of his early priorities was securing an extension with Russian President Vladimir Putin, making the issue part of his first major diplomatic conversations with the Kremlin. The episode is another example Biden uses to illustrate what he considers the diplomatic challenges inherited from Trump's first presidency. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Oliver Pritchard.
news.summary: Joe Biden's new memoir reveals just how much Donald Trump loomed over his presidency.
news.author: Hannah Parry

news.title: A New Analysis Has a Troubling Explanation for the Republican Midterm Wipeout
news.text:
For the past two weeks, Republicans have been searching for an autopsy to explain how a blue tsunami wiped us out in the 2026 midterms. A new analysis by J.L. Partners may offer an answer. While earlier polls suggested Republican voters had swung sharply toward Democrats, this analysis points to a different explanation for the party’s 15-point slide from 2024 to 2026: too many Trump voters simply stayed home.

NYP: Trump Voters Who Stayed Home Cost GOP Midterms More than two-thirds of the “Blue Tsunami” election earlier this month was the result of Trump supporters staying home The analysis by pollster J.L. Partners — an Election Day survey of 1,000 registered voters, checked against more than 30,000 interviews conducted during the campaign — found that 35% of Trump’s 2024 voters didn’t cast a ballot on Nov. 3. Just 8% of Trump voters switched sides to back Democrats Their absence alone accounts for 10 points of the 15-point swing toward Democrats since 2024, the firm calculated. Voters who switched sides supplied the other five https://t.co/glS0Kl84X7— Politics & Poll Tracker 📡 (@PollTracker2024) November 16, 2026

According to the poll, just 22 percent of Kamala Harris voters sat out the midterms, compared to an astounding 35 percent of Trump voters. That turnout gap alone accounted for 10 points of the Republicans’ 15-point slide, or 67 percent of the gap. Republican defections only accounted for the remaining five points. And even without those defections, the study indicates that Republicans would still have lost both the House and the Senate. 

Warning after warning before the midterms stressed that the election would come down to turnout, but apparently, too few Republicans took that seriously. 

The drop-off was especially pronounced among Trump’s voters without college degrees, rural voters, and retirees. Among those who backed Trump in 2024, 46 percent of voters without a college degree, 39 percent of rural voters, and 44 percent of voters over 65 stayed home in 2026, helping usher in a Democrat majority.

35% of President Trump’s 2024 voters stayed home during the 2026 midterms, while 52% voted Republican and 8% switched to Democrats. Among Trump voters aged 18–29, 16% defected to Democrats, while lower Republican turnout accounted for roughly two-thirds of the overall Democratic swing. Follow: @AFpost— AF Post (@AFpost) November 17, 2026

The voters who switched, just eight percent of Trump’s 2024 voters, were overwhelmingly young, particularly Gen Z, male, nonwhite, and urban. But the findings also raise questions about whether this group is worth trying to keep in the Republican coalition. These voters viewed the Democratic Socialists of America favorably, with 44 percent approving and just 27 percent disapproving. 

Other findings confirm what was already clear: Democrats benefited from opposition to Trump, not necessarily enthusiasm for their own agenda. Voters who disapproved of the president backed Democrats by 90 percent to six percent, and half of Democrat voters described their vote as a rebuke of the administration rather than an endorsement of Democratic policies. 

Still, half of those who switched from Republican to Democrat retained a positive view of the Republican Party, suggesting an opening to win them back in 2028. The cost of living, which included gas prices, and the broader economy were voters’ leading concerns. 

The poll also suggests Democrats have less reason to celebrate than the results might imply. Just 16 percent supported another effort to impeach Trump, and only 30 percent believed Democrats had a presidential contender ready to run. Surprisingly, Arizona Senator Mark Kelly performed best among the potential contenders tested with 2026 Democrat voters.

With turnout driving the Republican loss, the central question is why so many Republican voters stayed home. 

A sharp drop from a presidential election to a midterm is hardly unusual. Nearly 63 million voters backed Trump in 2016, compared with 50.5 million who voted Republican in 2018. In 2020, Trump won 74.2 million votes, while Republicans drew 54.2 million in the 2022 midterms. Trump’s total climbed to 77.3 million in 2024, but Republican turnout fell to roughly 50.1 million two weeks ago.

Whether that decline simply follows a familiar pattern or reflects deeper dissatisfaction with the Republican Party among its own voters remains unclear.

news.title: Joe Biden Reveals AOC Urged Him to Stay in 2024 Presidential Race Amid Secret Democratic Plot to Oust Him and Block Kamala Harris From Nomination
news.text:
Joe Biden is revealing the surprising Democratic allies who wanted him to stay in the 2024 presidential race, even as many of his party's top power players urged him to drop out, RadarOnline.com can reveal. 

In his new presidential memoir, Promise Me, America, the 83-year-old reveals that New York Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was among his defenders, urging him to stay in the White House race against Donald Trump even after his disastrous June debate performance sparked Democratic Party concerns.Joe Biden Didn't Want to 'Limp' to Democratic Presidential NominationBiden explained his agonizing decision to announce on July 21, 2024, that he wouldn't seek a second term, three months ahead of the general election.

"Admittedly, I had not started the year thinking that I would be withdrawing my candidacy for president. I know I opened the door with my performance at the debate. I could have fought to the convention. Taken the fight to the floor. Forced a vote. And probably prevailed," the former president wrote.

"After all, I had over 3,900 delegates. At the time, I needed 1,976. But I didn’t want to be a battered and bruised nominee leading a divided party. I wanted a united party," he continued. "I didn’t want a nominee who limped to the nomination. I wanted a nominee who would leave the convention with the wind at their back."Kamala Harris Was the 'Best Person to Be President If I Couldn't'After announcing his exit from the race, Biden immediately endorsed his Vice President, Kamala Harris, as the perfect candidate to move to the top of the ticket. 

"I picked Kamala Harris in 2020 because I believed she would be the best person to be president if I couldn’t do the job. I endorsed her quickly because there were strong voices in the party clamoring for a contested open primary," Biden penned.

"I didn’t think that was practical or wise," the 46th prez said. "It reflected a huge blind spot regarding the base of the party, and who was going to be in the hall as delegates in Chicago. Any contested open fight would have been seen as an attempt to block the first Black female vice president from the top of the ticket, and it would have split the party."AOC Threw Her Support Behind Joe Biden"A significant number of Democratic leaders did not want Kamala to be the nominee," Biden revealed before discussing how progressive "squad" member Ocasio-Cortez, 37, felt there were members of their party who wanted to oust both the president and Harris from running against Trump. 

"Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who had urged me to stay in the race, had already said publicly that the behind-the-scenes effort in the party wasn’t only to run me out of the race but to prevent Kamala from being the nominee," he shared.Biden's Instincts Helped Avoid a 'Fight' at 2024 DNC ConventionBiden's instincts to push Harris as his successor proved correct, as he later learned that an open primary would have caused chaos at the 2024 DNC convention. 

"After the election, the longtime Democratic strategist and party leader Donna Brazile and other prominent Black women in the party said as much when they stated that if there had been a fight at the convention and Kamala hadn’t been the nominee, they would have walked out," he wrote.

Biden added that two Democratic governors, who were reportedly angling for the nomination, got the message.

"Some prominent figures like Gretchen Whitmer and California Governor Gavin Newsom understood that," he explained. "That’s why they took their names out of the running preemptively."
news.summary: In his new presidential memoir, Joe Biden shared details on the drama leading up to the 2024 DNC convention.

news.title: It’s Time for Democrats to Put Up or Shut Up on Abortion Rights
news.text:
A historic blue wave has raised questions about what Democrats will do with their majority in both houses of Congress. With a Republican president in office, there will be limits on what the new congressional majority can accomplish, not least on reproductive rights. But there are opportunities for the party to make progress before 2029 if Democrats use their power with purpose.

Pundits sometimes suggest that voters have moved past the abortion issue, even though data suggest that reproductive rights were a key issue for some voters. The truth is far more complicated. A network of shield laws ensures that abortion remains broadly available, even in states that criminalize it. Voters perhaps paid less attention to abortion this cycle because no major policy change was making headlines, but ballot initiatives protecting abortion rights—three of four of which were successful this fall—show voters still care. And reproductive rights remain under threat. The Trump administration may act to end telehealth access to medication abortion by March 2027; federal lawsuits filed by the attorneys general of Louisiana, Idaho and Missouri, and Texas and Florida seek to take abortion pills off the market or reimpose restrictions that the Food and Drug Administration lifted. Other challenges to shield laws are in the pipeline, some of them predicated on the Comstock Act, a 19th-century obscenity law that some conservatives interpret as a de facto national abortion ban.

Reproductive-rights policies have featured prominently in Democrats’ plans for the first 100 days of a new Congress, and if the party doesn’t act on that agenda, Democrats could fall into a familiar trap: waiting to act until there’s a conservative victory in the federal courts or anti-abortion action by the executive branch. Democrats have done this in the past, missing opportunities to pass landmark legislation in the Clinton and Obama administrations. With the dust settling on the midterm, Democrats should ensure that history does not repeat itself.

Skeptics will stress that Donald Trump is still in the White House. The president will likely veto most bills passed by the Democratic majority, which will fall well short of the two-thirds needed to override.

But Trump hardly seems passionate about reproductive issues, and it’s possible to imagine him signing a bill that goes some way to loosen abortion restrictions. Last year, for example, he suggested that the party should be open to changing the Hyde Amendment, which bars most Medicaid reimbursement for abortion—a statement that has increasingly worried abortion opponents. And Medicaid coverage matters a great deal. Sixteen states where abortion is legal prohibit most Medicaid reimbursement, and groups offering private alternatives, like abortion funds, have struggled to fundraise in recent years. Cost is a major barrier for abortion-seekers, most of whom are low-income. The Hyde Amendment is part of appropriation riders for the Department of Health and Human Services; Democrats could remove it without repealing or amending an existing law.

Democrats also could wield the appropriations power to attack the Comstock Act, seeking to prohibit the Department of Justice from using funds to enforce it against those mailing or receiving abortion-related items. It could cost Trump politically for refusing to sign must-pass legislation because of an abortion-related provision, and thus shutting down the government.

Nevertheless, Trump could block most bills passed by the Democratic Congress. But a veto has consequences for Republicans. Each one will put Trump and congressional Republicans on record in rejecting a position that voters keep backing at the ballot box. Trump has successfully finessed the abortion issue since the start of the 2024 campaign, postponing federal action and avoiding discussion of his own views on the issue. Forcing a veto of a popular bill would remind voters of what the president’s party thinks—especially as the GOP begins to imagine a future after Trump leaves office. The leading candidates to top the ticket for the party in 2028, J.D. Vance and Marco Rubio, are far more conservative than Trump on abortion, and drawing out their views on reproductive health as part of a national conversation could be politically damaging in the future. Republicans who vote against these bills, or who defend current restrictions, will have to own that choice going into 2028.

A bill that fails now, moreover, is still worth writing because it will become a template for the moment when passage is possible. Democrats could propose legislation that includes and goes beyond restoring a federal right to abortion. Such a bill might face a filibuster since Democrats likely will not have 60 votes in the Senate, or the desire to end the filibuster altogether. But that shouldn’t change the imperative of drafting a compelling bill for future Congresses. In the past, Democrats with control of Congress and the White House have struggled to come together around a bill that is both pragmatic and principled. Advancing legislation of this kind could build coalitions among providers, advocates, labor, faith groups, and state officials, among others. A bill would also give members a record to run on, and gives voters a concrete sense of what could happen if Democrats win again in 2028. When Joe Biden and then Kamala Harris ran on reproductive rights in 2024, they struggled because the Democrats did not have a clear enough answer about what they could change if they held power. The new Congress can avoid the same pitfall by outlining a bold vision of its own.

That vision could go beyond a bill protecting abortion. Democrats could renew efforts to protect access to and reduce the costs of infertility treatments, like in vitro fertilization, and contraception. Democrats could try to preempt the weaponization of the Comstock Act by forcing a vote to repeal its provisions on abortion. The new congressional majority could help blue states in the interstate conflict over shield laws and mailed-medication abortion. State shield laws sometimes contain provisions establishing that the “site” of care is where the provider operates, not where the patient lives. A federal equivalent, potentially applying to telehealth care more broadly, could provide additional security and support for shield doctors serving patients in ban states.

More broadly, Democrats can offer their perspective on what it means to be pro-family. Republicans increasingly equate being pro-life and pro-family with ratcheting up criminal and civil penalties for those seeking certain healthcare treatments. Democrats could present an alternative by using the budget reconciliation process to address issues from prenatal care and paid family leave to extending postpartum coverage under Medicaid and supporting childcare and early education.

If Democrats want to avoid the threat of a filibuster, they may try to weave reproductive-rights measures into bills through appropriations or budget reconciliation, which allows Congress to pass spending, tax, and debt-limit legislation with a simple majority.

The Senate’s Byrd Rule limits what can be accomplished through reconciliation, requiring that a bill have a direct, non-incidental impact on federal spending or revenues. That would likely rule out a bill creating a new federal right to abortion or even Comstock Act repeal. That said, there are clear steps Democrats could attempt through reconciliation, notwithstanding the chances of a veto. For example, Democrats could seek to change the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act, originally passed through budget reconciliation, to withhold or reduce funding for hospitals that refuse to offer abortion as stabilizing treatment.

Democrats also can vote down federal abortion restrictions, such as efforts to block funding for Planned Parenthood or Title X family planning. Perhaps most significantly, a Democratic House can refuse to pass bills with anti-abortion riders such as the Hyde Amendment.

At the agency level, even though Congress cannot dictate the outcome, a Democratic majority can assess the FDA’s review of mifepristone, one of the two pills used in a majority of abortions nationwide, and one of the most studied drugs in the nation, with a safety record established since FDA approval in 2000. Under pressure from abortion opponents, the FDA launched its own new safety study and will issue a report no later than March 2027, after which it will decide on any changes. Democrats can intervene in several ways. First, committees can evaluate the review’s protocol, data, and communications with outside groups. They can ask who designed it and whether anti-abortion advocates influenced it. Such scrutiny might make it harder for the agency to publish a report that looks predetermined. The Trump administration may ignore these requests unless a court forces compliance, but committees can take important steps toward understanding the process that might lead to new FDA restrictions. Second, Democrats control the spending bills that fund the FDA. They can attach riders or reporting requirements to the FDA’s budget, or limit funds for changing mifepristone’s regulatory status if change is contrary to established evidence on safety. A caveat: Any such rider would have to survive negotiations with a president who can veto the bill. But taking both actions could matter in court and inform the current litigation asking courts to reimpose restrictions on mifepristone.

Finally, there’s Congressional approval of presidential nominations. Whether for the bench or for federal agencies, confirmation hearings can spotlight candidates’ views on reproductive rights. And a Democratic Senate can block or stall judicial nominees that committee members believe are unqualified for the position.

It may be tempting to believe that Democrats are better off focusing exclusively on issues like the cost of living and corruption that were also salient for voters. Democrats would be foolish not to try to deliver on those priorities. But there is no reason that the party cannot tackle reproductive rights at the same time, as they’ve outlined in their own health plans. Democrats have signaled to U.S. women that their health is a legislative priority, not just a talking point. Now that Roe v. Wade is gone and shield laws are at risk, it is time for the party to show that it meant what it said.
news.summary: A historic blue wave has raised questions about what Democrats will do with their majority in both houses of Congress.

news.title: Joe Biden Claims Donald Trump Admitted He Was 'Relieved' Not to Face Him in 2024 Election — After Ex-Prez Dropped Out Following Disastrous Debate Performance
news.text:
Joe Biden claims in his new presidential memoir that Donald Trump privately admitted he was "relieved" he didn't have to face off against the former president in the 2024 election, despite publicly bashing his longtime political rival, RadarOnline.com can reveal. 

Biden, 83, dropped out of the race in July 2024 following his poor debate performance against Trump, 80, the month before. He was replaced on the top of the ticket by his Vice President, Kamala Harris, who would overwhelmingly lose to the real estate mogul in November of that year.Joe Biden Claims Trump Made Stunning Admission to HimIn Promise Me, America, released on Tuesday, November 17, Biden writes about a meeting with Trump at the White House eight days after the election, where he said, "I honored another presidential tradition by hosting a visit from the president-elect."

While Trump's wife, Melania, skipped the traditional meeting, Biden and his wife, Jill, met the Don and his entourage in the Diplomatic Reception Room before the two leaders headed to the Oval Office, accompanied only by their respective chiefs of staff, Jeff Zients and Susie Wiles.

"He and I sat in chairs near a roaring fire; Jeff and Susie sat on sofas," Biden described, noting that Trump seemed "immediately chatty," to the degree that the former Delaware Senator "thought he might be putting me on."Joe Biden Said Trump Confided His 'Relief' About Not Facing Him in ElectionBiden claimed that Trump told him that "he was relieved he didn’t have to run against me" in the 2024 election. 

"I didn’t really understand why he was buttering me up," he added.

"I cut off his compliments to move on to the business at hand," Biden continued. "I wanted to give him a wide-ranging overview of the issues that I thought would dominate his presidency, because a lot had happened since January 2021."

Trump publicly admitted he much preferred facing off against Harris instead of Biden after the former president formally abandoned his reelection bid on July 21, 2024, just over three months before Election Day. But the Republican changed his tune after his landslide victory, scoffing at the idea that Biden ever stood a chance of beating him.Donald Trump Said He'd 'Rather Run Against' Kamala Harris"I always felt he was incompetent, but he had a certain base. And no matter how bad he was, people are gonna vote for him. She doesn't have that base," Trump explained about voting patterns in a July 29, 2024, interview with Fox News' Laura Ingraham

"Everybody knows who I am, and now people know who she is. She's a radical left lunatic. She'll destroy our country. She wants open borders," he claimed about his then-new opponent, Harris. 

Trump doubled down at an August 9, 2024, campaign rally in Montana, telling the crowd, "I'd rather run against her. I think she's easier to beat. I really do."Donald Trump Later Said Biden Wouldn't Have Had a 'Chance'However, Trump later changed his tune about a potential rematch with Biden, who had defeated him in the 2020 election.

The President-elect scoffed at the idea that Biden could have beaten him again while chatting with reporters at his Mar-a-Lago New Year's Eve bash, just three weeks before returning to the White House for a second term.

"Well, he was way behind," he said at the time. "He would've really, I assume, not had a chance."
news.summary: Joe Biden claims Donald Trump made the private admission to him during the traditional Oval Office visit just days after the 2024 election.

The Democrats have won the battle, but now the fight for the party's future begins

After a major midterm victory, Democrats face a showdown over Senate leadership, a battle to deliver for voters and an increasingly crowded race to take on Trump in 2028.

7.26pm, 17 Nov 2026

Share options

Marion McKeone

TO PARAPHRASE BENDAN Behan, the first item on the Democrats agenda, following their most decisive triumph in half a century, is the split.

Jubilant and flushed with victory, they arrived in their thousands to ‘What’s Next?’ a three-day jamboree of newly minted Senators, wannabe presidential contenders, strategists, activists, leaders and Democratic veterans.

The event was the brainchild of Lis Smith, a 41-year-old Democratic strategist who has notched up 20 victories in less than a decade.

1/5 Less than 18 months after launching @MajorityDems , we just wrapped our "What's Next" event in Denver.

3,500 attendees. 130 elected officials from 39 states. Nearly 100 program participants.

Pretty awesome to see what we've built.— Lis Smith (@Lis_Smith) November 14, 2026

Smith was behind the campaigns of three of the biggest – and unlikeliest – of midterm winners; Josh Turek in Iowa, Alex Hamilton in Kansas and James Talarico in Texas.

When I first heard she was involved with their campaigns, I was tempted to bet $100 on a winning trifecta. Had I done so, I’d be sipping a cocktail somewhere sunny instead of cranking out this column.

Senate leadership

To answer their own question, what’s next – and it’s already taking place – is the first open battle over the Senate leadership since 1994.

Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen’s challenge to Chuck Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for more than a decade, sets the stage for a battle between the party’s sclerotic old guard and progressives who have chafed under a decade of Schumer’s timid leadership.

Chris Van Hollen, left, and Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

It’s less about age than ideas, and less about style than substance. Van Hollen is 67 to Schumer’s 75 years. He’s no firebrand; he has the measured delivery of a small-town solicitor. But he’s shown himself to be a courageous and principled leader who was willing to stand up to Trump while Schumer repeatedly ducked below the political parapet.

Advertisement

In April 2025, when America was reeling at the brutality of Trump’s anti-immigrant onslaught, he flew to El Salvador and demanded access to Kilmer Abrego Garcia, a legal US resident who had been deported to the notorious CECOT prison in direct violation of a judge’s order.

He’s one of a handful of Democratic Senators who consistently called for an end to unconditional military aid for Israel, long before public opinion shifted in line with his position. During fact-finding trips to the Rafah crossing, he excoriated Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for refusing to allow humanitarian aid into Gaza; and Biden and Trump for their failure to rein him in.

Back then Schumer’s supporters muttered that Van Hollen was all but ensuring a kamikaze end to his Senate career; today most Americans oppose the US’s willingness to allow Netanyahu and the IDF carte blanche in Gaza and the West Bank.

It’s not for nothing that Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders, no slouches when it comes to taking on the Trump administration, deride Schumer as the leader of the Senate ‘flight club.’ He’s a relic of a bygone era, a Biden holdover out of step with a newly invigorated Democratic Party and the newly elected Class of ’26.

Schumer has been taking an extended victory lap to celebrate the 56-44 turning of the Senate tide. But there’s a compelling a case to be made that the Democratic victories in Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, Michigan, Minnesota, Iowa and Maine happened despite Schumer’s role in selecting and funding Senate candidates, not because of it.

During primaries in Maine, Minnesota and Michigan he put his thumb on the scale for clearly inferior candidates. He failed to support James Talarico, Scott Colom, Alex Hamilton or Annie Andrews until it became clear they were heading for victory. And he ignored races in Louisiana and Florida, where cash-starved Democratic candidates came within an inch of defeating Republican opponents whose campaigns were awash with funds.

Schumer’s status quo approach seems increasingly out of step with public opinion and unlikely to consolidate the midterm gains in 2028. When it comes to Israel, both Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries, who are on track to become the next House Speaker, have been the recipients of AIPAC’s largesse. They’ve received donations from the same large financial and energy corporations that have bankrolled Trump.

It’s not clear that Van Hollen will win. Schumer, a veteran of the backroom deal, may agree to a compromise under which he would surrender the Senate leadership in 2028, in exchange for the next two years at the helm. By 2028 he may have no choice; Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is widely expected to challenge him for his New York Senate seat in a Democratic primary she would almost certainly win. New Yorkers haven’t forgiven him for refusing to endorse Zohran Mamdani, even after he won the Democratic primary.

A mountain to climb

There are other tussles taking place on the sidelines as Democrats seek to respond to voters demands for accountability and affordability. The investigations and oversight list is endless; Jared Kushner’s special envoy self-enrichment deals, Elon Musk’s Doge chaos and his throttling of Ukraine’s StarShield defence system, the Trump pardon industry, the corruption and chaos of privately run DHS detention centres, ICE’s lawless rampages, billions of dollars in Pentagon contracts awarded to companies connected to

Trump’s sons, the crypto scams, the Qatari jet, Jenson Huang’s honeypot scandal …. the list goes on.

Trump in the Philippines this week. Quad leaders, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi of Japan, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Trump and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

But as Brendan Boyle, the Democrats’ politically astute budget whiz points out, the immediate focus needs to be on big legislative swings that will show the American voters that Democrats understand their mandate is to lower costs and reduce the galloping inequality that fuelled the midterm revolt.

In truth, the blue wave had little to do with Democratic leaders in the House and Senate. The same impulses that drove millions of Americans to take part in No Kings marches across America propelled record numbers of Americans to the ballot boxes in protest at the cruelty, grift and incompetence of the Trump administration. It was a populist revolt against a President whose policies and tax cuts created almost 300 new billionaires in two years, while America’s wage earners accounted for the lowest percentage of GDP since 1929.

Democrats are mostly agreed that restoring the healthcare and welfare benefits that Trump gutted to fund billionaire tax breaks, blocking his tariffs and forcing an end to the war in Iran is a good place to start. With Iran, you suspect they may be pushing at an open door. Trump has long since lost interest in his war of whim; there’s probably nothing he’d like more than to be able to pin his inevitable, ignominious retreat on the Democrats.

Whether he wins or not, Van Hollen’s policies seem to reflect what Americans want; eliminating federal taxes for Americans making less than $46,000 (€42,000) a year, increasing taxes on corporations and the wealthy, restoring food subsidies to low-income families, expanding childcare and cutting off funding for the war in Iran.

Even with new leadership will be a limit to what they can achieve; Trump’s power of veto, his unlimited executive order powers and the recently expanded immunity courtesy of the Supreme Court means he can wreak plenty more havoc between now and 2028. But this time around, instead of ducking for cover, Democrats seem determined to go to the mat to fulfil their mandate.

The What’s Next? event suggests also served as a beauty pageant of sorts for the two dozen or so Democrats who are pondering a presidential run in 2028. Three quarters of Americans now live in states run by Democratic governors. This is significant because governors tend to win more Presidential elections than Senators. At least nine Democratic governors are expected to throw their hats into the primary ring early next year, including California governor Gavin Newsom, Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro and New Jersey governor Phil Murphy.

Expect Michigan governor Gretchen Whitmer, who claimed earlier this year she’s not interested, to change her mind. Whitmer, an effective and popular two-term governor in a swing state that voted twice for Trump, is leaving a Democratic trifecta in charge of Michigan. Jocelyn Benson, Whitmer’s former secretary of state, has been elected governor, Democrats control both houses in the state legislature and Abdul Al Sayed has just been elected as Michigan’s second Democratic senator. By any standard, that’s a formidable legacy for a Democrat in a swing state.

Don't discount Michigan Gov Gretchen Whitmer when looking at the primaries next year for Dems.Alamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff is leading the pack of at least eight senators who have expressed interest in running, along with Arizona Senator Mark Kelly and Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin. The remaining third is made up of former Cabinet members, Mayors and House Representatives. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, former Obama chief of staff Rahm Emanuel, former vice president Kamala Harris and New York Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez all belong to this group.

Expect Ossoff, Pritzker, Slotkin, Kelly, Shapiro and Whitmer to make the final round. Newsom, who easily ticks the national recognition and fundraising boxes, has said he won’t seek the nomination if Harris decides to run again. Which suggests Harris is less likely to declare her candidacy than Newsom.

More than anyone Ossoff represents the face of the new Democratic Party; a young, telegenic Senator with formidable communication skills who has just been reelected by a landslide in one of America’s most conservative states. But America likes presidents with a sense of humour, and Ossoff, who can come across as a scold, could use a little of Newsom’s levity.

news.title: Florida Hispanic Republicans Pick Rubio Over DeSantis for 2028, Poll Finds
news.text: Secretary of State Marco Rubio holds a commanding lead over Vice President JD Vance and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis among Hispanic Republicans in Florida in an early look at the 2028 GOP presidential primary, according to a new poll. The survey, conducted for HispanicsVote.org, found that 57 percent of Florida Hispanic Republicans would back Rubio, compared with 25 percent for DeSantis and 10 percent for Vance. Fewer than 4 percent were undecided. Former Virginia Governor Glenn Youngkin, the fourth candidate included in the survey, received no support. The primary question was asked only of the 351 registered Republicans in a sample of 855 Hispanic registered voters in Florida. The poll was conducted from October 14 to 18, more than two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, in which Democrats made gains with Latino voters in Florida but still lost statewide races. The full survey has a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points, while the margin of error for the Republican subgroup is wider. For the Republican subgroup, it is roughly plus or minus 5.2 points. Newsweek reached out to the State Department, the vice president's office and DeSantis's office for comment on Tuesday. Rubio's Home-State Edge Florida's Hispanic Republicans like all three men about the same, with Rubio, DeSantis and Vance each posting favorable ratings between 88 and 90 percent. The gap is in how strongly they feel. Seventy-two percent view Rubio very favorably and 73 percent say so of DeSantis, compared with 42 percent for Vance. If Rubio, son of Cuban immigrants and a former Florida senator, were the nominee, 61 percent of Hispanic Republicans said they would be much more motivated to vote in 2028. He also led California Governor Gavin Newsom 39 percent to 32 percent among all Florida Hispanic voters in a hypothetical general election. Barbara Casanova, founder of HispanicsVote.org and chair of the Republican National Hispanic Assembly in Florida, cautioned against reading too much into the Rubio numbers. "I really think that the field is still pretty wide open," she told Newsweek. "We would love to see the first Hispanic American in office at the highest level, but in Florida, there is a lot of support for DeSantis." National legislation and events could still move them before 2028, she said. "It's very, very early out." Casanova credited Rubio's work at the State Department, pointing to Cuba, Iran, Venezuela and recent elections in Colombia. If that run of foreign policy wins continues, she said, Rubio could be "a very strong candidate" with support from both sides. Rubio has gained ground this year but continues to trail Vance in national polling. He has publicly said he would step aside if Vance decides to run. DeSantis, who leaves office on January 5, when Governor-elect Byron Donalds takes office, has also gained ground. His recent moves have fueled speculation that he is positioning himself for another White House run. Cuban Americans made up about 46 percent of the Republican respondents, and the poll asked about the island. Among Hispanic Republicans, 53 percent said they favor active efforts to encourage political change and opposition movements inside Cuba. About 11 percent wanted more pressure and sanctions on the Cuban government, and 36 percent were unsure. A Rare Consensus on Immigration Support for a pathway to citizenship came close to unanimous in the survey. Ninety-seven percent of all respondents backed one for undocumented immigrants who have lived in the U.S. for a long time, pay taxes and have no serious criminal record, and Hispanic Republicans were at 93 percent. Deporting only immigrants convicted of felonies drew 91 percent support overall and 86 percent among Republicans. Most respondents rejected deporting long-term residents with no criminal record, including 58 percent of Republicans, and 69 percent overall opposed using appearance, language or type of work as a factor in immigration stops. More border security and enforcement had 53 percent support statewide, rising to 68 percent among Republicans. Asked how recent immigration actions such as raids and deportations had affected their community or family, 45 percent said the impact was negative. "They support securing the border and removing criminals, while also recognizing that long-term residents who work, pay taxes, and play by the rules should have a path to legal status," Casanova said in a statement. "That is not a soft policy. That is practical, pro-family, pro-work conservatism that matches how our community actually lives." Casanova separated border security from how it has been enforced. "Hispanic voters, almost across the board, support a closed border, very, very strong security at the border," she said. "But the issue has really been about the way it's been handled." She faulted the White House for its messaging. "I think the administration has not done a good job of communicating who is being deported, why and how they're being identified," Casanova said. In her view, many deportees described in the media as noncriminals came to the border seeking asylum and were given work permits and court dates years away, protections the federal government can revoke. Voters, she said, are uncomfortable with how Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have operated in local stores and other public places, even around legal immigrants. "It leaves a bad impression on our community and our voters," she said. "It hasn't changed how we feel about immigration and the need to have reform done, but it also creates distrust and misunderstandings and miscommunications." Casanova said she plans to seek a meeting with the office of Florida Representative María Elvira Salazar, a Republican, and other leaders to push for a new immigration policy. Salazar's own immigration plan "was not popular," she said, and getting both parties to agree on a fix is hard. "We know that it has to be done and citizens are really asking for a solution." Rubio knows the issue from his Senate days. In 2013, he was one of the bipartisan "Gang of Eight" senators who wrote an immigration overhaul with a path to citizenship. It passed the Senate and died in the House. Economic Strain and the Midterm Backdrop Most respondents described money trouble at home. Sixty-two percent said their families are worse off financially than a year ago, and 1.8 percent said they are better off. A majority, 54 percent, said Florida is on the wrong track. Republicans were more upbeat, with 30 percent saying they are worse off and 65 percent saying the state is headed in the right direction. On the American dream, 52 percent said it is not really or not at all attainable, the result Casanova called the poll's most significant. "To have results that showed a significant number of voters that saw the American dream is no longer attainable or only somewhat attainable, to me was very troubling," she said. Republicans held Florida on November 3, narrowly. Senator Ashley Moody won 51 percent to 48 percent and Donalds beat Democrat David Jolly 50 percent to 49 percent. Among Latino voters, a postelection UnidosUS survey found Democrat Angie Nixon beat Moody 53 percent to 43 percent and Jolly beat Donalds 53 percent to 41 percent. Jared Nordlund, Florida state director for UnidosUS, said Latino voters "are stretched to the limit, and they expect results." Miami-Dade County swung 18 points toward Democrats compared with the 2024 presidential race, according to The Associated Press, though Hispanic voters there still sided with Republicans by smaller margins than before. An earlier release from the same HispanicsVote.org survey showed Jolly ahead of Donalds 43 percent to 38 percent among Hispanic voters. "The enthusiasm is on the Democrat side. But Republicans have a machinery," Eduardo Gamarra, a political scientist at Florida International University, told NPR before the election. Democrats have their own worries about Rubio. "If Marco Rubio is the nominee for president, we are in trouble," Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego said in June at a Latino Vote Summit in Washington. Ocasio-Cortez Leads on the Democratic Side Among the 306 Hispanic Democrats surveyed, New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez led a 2028 Democratic primary with 44 percent. Former Vice President Kamala Harris was second with 22 percent, followed by Newsom at 14 percent and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 9 percent. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear registered no support, and 11 percent were undecided. "There was oddly a lot of support for AOC, which I thought unusual," Casanova said. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Oliver Pritchard.
news.summary: Rubio holds a wide lead over DeSantis among Florida Hispanic Republicans in an early 2028 poll, with Vance a distant third.
news.author: Jesus Mesa

news.title: Ex-Trump Supporter Comedian Accuses Prez of 'Corruption' as He Brands Him the 'Greatest Failure'
news.text:
Comedian Andrew Schulz, who voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election and gave him a major podcast platform during the campaign, is now accusing the president of betraying his promises.

Schulz, 43, delivered his latest criticism on the November 14 episode of The Brilliant Idiots, a YouTube podcast he co-hosts with radio personality Charlamagne tha God. During the taping, he claimed that the Democrats’ victories in the November midterm elections represented a rejection of MAGA, RadarOnline can report.'Greatest Failure of a President'Reflecting on the midterm election results, Charlamagne noted, “I don’t necessarily think it was a blue wave. I just think it was a complete rebuke of the last decade of MAGA. That’s all.” 

He pointed to Democratic victories in South Carolina, Kansas, Mississippi and Texas as evidence of Trump’s political failures.

“He completely, without a shadow of a doubt, blew it as a president,” Charlamagne added.

Schulz agreed, describing Trump’s presidency as the “greatest failure of a president” of his lifetime.

“The point being, like, it is the greatest fall from grace, miscalculation, the greatest failure,” he continued.

Schulz acknowledged that politicians regularly make promises they fail to fulfill but argued that Trump’s actions went beyond ordinary political disappointments.

“What is more rare is literally doing the exact opposite of the things that you campaign on to a level that nobody’s seen before and a level of corruption and cronyism that has never been seen in Western democracy,” Schulz said. “I think the main thing was that he recognized what Americans actually care about and want, and then did the exact opposite of all those things.”Schulz Voted for Trump After Giving Him a Podcast PlatformSchulz’s latest criticism is notable given his previous support for Trump during the 2024 presidential campaign. The New York-born comedian was among the podcast personalities who helped the Republican reach younger male audiences.

Trump appeared on Schulz’s Flagrant podcast in October 2024 for an approximately 90-minute interview that attracted more than 9 million YouTube views, with other reports putting the figure near 10 million.

Schulz subsequently confirmed that he voted for Trump, despite previously identifying as a lifelong Democrat.

In a June 21, 2025, interview with The New York Times, Schulz explained that his vote was primarily a rejection of the Democratic establishment.

“I voted for Trump, yeah, but my vote was more like I voted against a Democratic institution that I feel was stripping the democratic process from its constituents,” Schulz said. “I didn’t like the way things were going, and Kamala (Harris) was saying, yeah, we’re going to keep doing that."‘I Voted for None of This’Schulz began publicly expressing disappointment with Trump after the president returned to the White House in January 2025. By July, he was criticizing the administration for pursuing policies he believed contradicted the promises that earned his support.

During an episode of Flagrant, Schulz recalled receiving messages from people reminding him that he had voted for Trump.

“There’ll be people… they’ll DM me like, ‘You see what your boy’s doing? You voted for this.’ I’m like, ‘I voted for none of this,’” Schulz said. “He’s doing the exact opposite of everything I voted for.” 

“If you bring up another f---ing pedophile about deporting and you’re not releasing the Epstein list, just shut the f--- up, all of you.”

Schulz’s criticism expanded in January 2026 following the fatal shootings of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis. The comedian described the administration’s response as a breaking point, arguing that the incidents reinforced his concerns about Trump’s approach to executive power.From New York Comedy Clubs to Podcast StardomBorn in New York City, Schulz built his career through stand-up performances, television appearances and digital media. 

He began performing comedy while attending college and continued pursuing stand-up after returning to New York, becoming a regular at local comedy clubs. He made his Edinburgh Comedy Festival debut in 2008 and later gained television exposure through MTV’s Guy Code franchise.

Schulz also developed an online following through independently released comedy projects, including 4:4:1 (2017), 5:5:1 (2018) and Infamous (2022). His more recent projects include the 2025 special Life and a role as Dan Hibiki in the 2026 Street Fighter adaptation.
news.summary: A former Trump voter and comedian has turned against the president, accusing him and his administration of 'corruption.'
news.author: Christian Spencer

news.title: Did 'The Simpsons' predict a Nov. 17 blackout? What the episode shows
news.text:
"The Simpsons" is fueling another round of prediction chatter, this time over a fictional blackout.

A clip from the animated comedy's 2023 episode "It's a Blunderful Life" has resurfaced as users connect its Nov. 17 reference to rumors about a widespread power outage. But the episode does not identify 2026 as the year of a predicted blackout.

In the episode, Lisa Simpson looks back on a power failure that left Springfield without electricity before Thanksgiving, with Homer taking the blame. She flips through her diary and lands on the date marked Nov. 17, which includes an entry referencing an approaching storm. FX's official episode listing⁠ identifies "It's a Blunderful Life" as Season 35's seventh episode, which originally aired Nov. 19, 2023.

Did 'The Simpsons' predict Apple's Vision Pro? Product is eerily similar to fictional device

The Federal Emergency Management Agency and Federal Communications Commission have scheduled their nationwide Emergency Alert System test⁠ for approximately 2:20 p.m. ET Nov. 17. Participating broadcasters and other providers will interrupt programming to carry the test message, then resume regular programming. No nationwide power shutdown is scheduled.

"This is only a test. No action is required by the public," the message will say, according to FEMA. The agency says the exercise evaluates whether providers can receive and relay emergency messages.

Some social media users have linked FEMA's Nov. 17 test to the episode's fictional blackout, fueling fears of a real power outage. However, FEMA's test checks emergency communications without shutting off electricity, making the likelihood of a blackout slim. 

The purpose of the test is to allow FEMA to assess the Emergency Alert System, which is one way the agency can distribute alerts during a national emergency.

'The Simpson's predictions have sparked conversations

The show's reputation for anticipating real events has fueled similar discussions before.

In 2024⁠ viewers compared Apple's Vision Pro with headsets worn by Springfield residents in the 2016 episode "Friends and Family." A tiger attack depicted in a 1993 episode also preceded the 2003 mauling of entertainer Roy Horn during a Siegfried & Roy performance.

In 2024, longtime writer on the show, Al Jean, made a post comparing Lisa's presidential outfit with Kamala Harris' purple ensemble and pearls at the 2021 inauguration⁠.

"'Prediction' I'm proud to be a part of," Jean wrote on X at the time.

Other supposed predictions have been proven to be false. Fact checks debunked claims involving the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot, Queen Elizabeth II's death, the monkeypox outbreak, Silicon Valley Bank's collapse and a "solar superstorm."

Former showrunner Bill Oakley told Reuters in 2020 that the writers often satirize earlier events. "Because history keeps repeating, it just seems like we were predicting things," he said.

Contributing: James Powel, USA TODAY
