news.title: Republican Governor-Elect Nominates Lifelong Democrat To Be His Attorney General
news.text:
Republican Wyoming Gov.-elect Eric Barlow nominated a lifelong Democrat to be his state attorney general. 

Barlow nominated attorney Walter Eggers to be the next attorney general, who donated over $20,000 to Democrats in recent decades, Federal Elections Commission (FEC) filings show. Liberal donors, advocacy groups and corporate interests collectively played a key role in helping Barlow secure the Republican nomination and in ousting conservatives with liberal Republicans. 

Eggers confirmed to The Cowboy State Daily that he has been a lifelong Democrat. He argued that the difference between Democrats and Republicans in Wyoming is not as great as people suggest. 

Eggers donated $1,000 to former President Joe Biden’s campaign on Feb. 29, 2020, and $2,300 to former President Barack Obama’s campaign in 2008, FEC filings show. He donated over $18,000 to the Wyoming Democratic Party between 2004 and 2020. (RELATED: Grassroots Wyoming Conservatives Coalescing Around New Governor Candidate To Defeat Left-Leaning GOP Nominee)

Per FEC records, Eggers has given: $18,735 to the Wyoming Democratic Party (2004-2020) $2,300 to Barack Obama $1,800 to the DNC $1,250 to Hillary Clinton $1,000 to Joe Biden $250 to Kamala Harris (2024) For years, the state party got a check almost every month.— State Freedom Caucus Network (@SFC_Network) November 16, 2026

Barlow did not immediately respond to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s request for comment. 

Barlow defeated Megan Degenfelder, who President Donald Trump endorsed, during the Aug. 18 primary. The Wyoming Freedom Caucus lost its majority in the state House after 13 incumbent members were defeated and four additional Freedom Caucus-aligned members lost their state Senate bids. 

The governor-elect defeated Democratic Wyoming gubernatorial candidate Ken Casner and Constitution Party candidate Rebecca Bextel with 68.1% of the vote. Bextel, who launched her campaign after the primary, came in second with 16.6% of the vote. Bextel told the DCNF that she launched her campaign to stop the left-leaning Barlow from becoming governor. 

“People understand how desperate it is,” Bextel told the DCNF in September. “So yes, I need all the help I can get, but I am fully expecting to win this race. And look, this should bring hope to everybody in Wyoming. If the establishment Republicans and establishment Democrats want the same thing, it takes the rest of us to fight for the American people.”

Barlow voted with a majority of Democrats 90% of the time and was the sixth most liberal Republican in the state House, according to Evidence Based Wyoming’s Doug Gerard. He was affiliated with the anti-coal, anti-oil and anti-gas Powder River Basin Resource Council. 

The governor-elect voted to raise taxes on the oil and gas industry, sponsored an amendment in 2014 to accept Obamacare funding in Wyoming and voted to change the definition of marriage, according to Gerard’s report.

Barlow received more than $1,000 from Rene Hinkle, a plaintiff in lawsuits challenging Wyoming’s abortion ban, according to Cowboy State Daily. A Barlow campaign spokeswoman said the donation and others reflected “what [Barlow] stands for. Which is respectful leadership. And he has a record on that.”

The Wyoming Donor Alliance, a non-partisan organization, outlined a plan to oust Freedom Caucus and Trump-endorsed candidates to replace them with less conservative Republicans. It created a strategy titled, “Break the Wyoming Freedom Caucus Majority,” according to documentation previously obtained by the DCNF. 

The plan intended to raise $839,500 to recruit candidates, target specific voters and endorse or oppose Freedom Caucus candidates. 

Wayne Hughes Jr., the owner of Cowboy State Daily, gave $15,000 to the Civil Leadership PAC, which spent about $200,000 backing non-Freedom Caucus Republicans in the primary, according to Transparency USA. The Civil Leadership PAC backed Short and Barlow, which Neiman and other conservatives argued were not true conservatives. 

The PAC spent $168,000 in expenditures to support Barlow’s gubernatorial bid, $19,000 to support Short and over $4,000 on Republican Wyoming state Rep. Steve Harshman, who won his primary in hopes of becoming the next superintendent of public instruction. Harshman defeated Republican Wyoming state Rep. Tom Kelly, who was backed by the Freedom Caucus, according to Cowboy State Daily.

A newly formed PAC called Common Sense Republicans for Wyoming endorsed Barlow and candidates running against Freedom Caucus members.
news.summary: Egger has donated thousands of dollars to Democrats
news.author: Nicole Silverio

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed 2028 Chances as Dem Strategist Sees Him as AOC Alternative
news.text: Democratic strategist Dan Turrentine said there is "almost a consensus" within his party that Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed would run for president in 2028 if Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who is seen as the favorite among many progressives, opts against standing. He said he saw the near consensus during the What’s Next conference, Democrats’ post-election conference in Denver, Colorado, over the weekend. He made the comments during a new episode of The Huddle podcast. "Because we have no front-runner, because we don’t even know if AOC is going to run, there’s increasing talk—one of the things when I left Saturday morning, there was almost a consensus that if AOC doesn’t run, El-Sayed is," he said. But El-Sayed has said he is "not running" and wants to focus on his job in the Senate. Turrentine's comments come just weeks after El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race by about 7 points, a major victory for the progressive left in one of the nation’s most closely divided swing states. With the midterms in the rearview, 2028 speculation has already begun in Washington. Democrats are preparing to launch presidential runs over the coming months as the party grapples with the direction it should take following their significant wins over Republicans earlier this month. Ocasio-Cortez, of New York, is frequently named as a potential presidential candidate who could consolidate support on the Democratic Party’s left due to her status as a well-known national figure who is popular among Democrats. But she has also been floated as a potential primary challenger to New York Senator Chuck Schumer, a Democrat who has caught the ire of the party’s progressive base. If Ocasio-Cortez chooses not to run for president, she may leave a gap in the primary, as it’s less clear who would be able to run in that progressive lane, which was occupied by Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders in 2016 and 2020. El-Sayed is among the left-leaning politicians who have been named as potential candidates. Abdul El-Sayed Downplayed 2028 Speculation El-Sayed, for his part, has downplayed speculation that he could run for 2028. He told progressive news outlet Zeteo after his victory he is "not running" for president and that his job is to be the "best senator" he can be. The incoming senator would face a difficult path to victory if he chooses to run due to what would be a very short stint in the Senate prior to his campaign, Todd Belt, director of the Political Management Program at The George Washington University, told Newsweek on Tuesday. "Democrats in the primaries will be looking for somebody who has some experience at delivering, and it's highly unlikely that El-Sayed will be able to have any sort of record of delivering within just a couple of years, maybe not even that, of being in the Senate without a filibuster-proof majority and a president who is guaranteed to veto quite a bit of the legislation that he would like to pass," he said. Democratic strategist Eddie Vale told Newsweek he is more skeptical about El-Sayed running. "He was just elected to Senate of course but I also think there is a much better case that he can build power and advocate for what he wants by being a key voice in the primary and general election in Michigan, and having other candidates seek out his support rather than throwing his hat in the ring and instantly becoming a target for everyone," he said. Newsweek reached out to El-Sayed’s team for comment via email. Abdul El-Sayed’s Chances in 2028 Post-midterms polling on El-Sayed’s chances in 2028 has been limited, but one survey from The New York Times and Siena University published prior to the elections signaled that he would have a tough time in the primary field. Prediction markets are also not bullish on his chances. El-Sayed’s chances stood at less than half a percentage point in the Times poll, which surveyed 1,170 registered voters from October 12 to 19. Instead, it gave an edge to former Vice President Kamala Harris, who had support from 12 percent of respondents, followed by California Governor Gavin Newsom at 9 percent, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 7 percent and Ocasio-Cortez at 6 percent. Most voters—45 percent—were undecided. El-Sayed’s chances were also low on prediction markets—having just a 0.7 percent chance on Kalshi and a 1 percent chance on Polymarket as of Tuesday morning. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. Is Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez Running for President? Prominent progressives weighing presidential runs could be waiting to see what Ocasio-Cortez ultimately decides to do in 2028. She could run for president, challenge Schumer or even run for reelection to her House seat in New York’s 14th Congressional District. She has filed paperwork with the Federal Election Commission (FEC) to run for a sixth term in the House, but has not said for sure what her next steps will be. The filing on its own does not necessarily mean she will run for reelection—it only signals that she is keeping her options open. In September, she told the Times she expected to decide on a presidential run after the midterms. "I’m not naive to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latin," Ocasio-Cortez said. "And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities." Ocasio-Cortez previously addressed presidential speculation last May in a conversation with David Axelrod, a former adviser to former President Barack Obama. "My ambition is to change this country," she said. "Presidents come and go. Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go. But single-payer healthcare is forever. A living wage is forever, workers' rights are forever, women's rights, all of that, and so anyways…to a finer point to your question is that when you aren't attached, when you haven't been like fantasizing about being this or that since the time you were seven years old, it is tremendously liberating." The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) passed a resolution titled "Run AOC 2028 To Win A Democratic Socialist President" during its November 14 convention, reported City & State New York. Could the Left Win in 2028? Debate over the direction of the party has already begun ahead of the next presidential election. Questions over whether progressives can actually win a national presidential contest have always been a point of contention for the left. Many Democrats believe someone who is more moderate will be better suited to win over independent voters and centrist Republicans. Progressives, however, believe someone on the left could convince disaffected Democrats to head to the polls. They argue midterm results, such as El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan or Maine Senator-elect Troy Jackson’s victory over Republican Senator Susan Collins in Maine, suggest that progressives can indeed win tough races. Belt said that progressives are in a better strategic position in terms of how they have conducted their campaigns ahead of 2028, even if that is not necessarily true in terms of policy. "The one thing I will say about the progressives is they are giving people something to vote for and not just against. That's something that the moderates and the establishment have really focused on, is stopping Trump. Okay, but how are you going to put money back in people's pockets?" he said. Still, he noted that the map is going to be tough for the left. South Carolina, a state where voters tend to be more liberal economically but socially moderate, will be the first state to have their primaries in 2028. "It's going to be difficult for a progressive to get out of the primaries and to win the nomination. And a lot of times the money backs the safe candidate. That's, you know, what we saw with Biden in 2020," he said. Still, primaries don’t always come down to the progressive vs. moderate debate, he said, noting that ultimately what matters is any individual candidate and their message. "Somebody like an Obama, it almost doesn't matter where they are politically," he said. Who Else Could Compete for the Progressive Lane? If Ocasio-Cortez opts against running, it’s not clear who would become the progressive front-runner. Many of the leading candidates such as Harris, Newsom, Buttigieg and Ossoff are seen as more moderate Democrats. Sanders has not indicated he would run again, and many progressives have argued it’s time for a younger generation of leaders. At 85, his age could become a concern for progressive voters. Representative Ro Khanna, a California Democrat, is another progressive who has been floated as a presidential candidate but has also trailed in polls. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is ineligible because he does not meet the "natural-born citizen" requirement outlined in Article II of the United States Constitution. Vale said a major lesson from the midterms is that "people don't neatly break down on the ideological lines and litmus tests of folks in DC." "A lot of the candidates who won I would consider more progressive on some issues and more moderate on other issues they don't neatly fit into groups' boxes. And that ability to transcend the policy/political lines will be key to winning," he said. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Robert Greenall and Samantha Beech
news.summary: Strategist Dan Turrentine said there is "almost a consensus" among Democrats El-Sayed will run if AOC passes on 2028.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: ‘Gayest’ Member of Congress Robert Garcia Devotes Quarter of Oversight Staff to Videos, Influencer Outreach
news.text:
Democrat Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA), who once referred to himself as the “gayest” member of Congress, is reportedly using a quarter of committee resources to focus not on affordability but communication, zoning in on influencers, TikTok videos, and more in what has been described as a “presidential-style communication shop.”

Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, is among Democrats who openly admitted that he plans to target Trump officials when Democrats take back power — something Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) and others warned would happen ahead of the midterms. During a recent Crooked Con event in Washington, DC, Garcia essentially attributed this desire, in part, to his so-called “gay… pettiness.”

“Just because you’re Kimberly Guilfoyle, or you’re Kristi Noem, or you’re Pam Bondi, and you’re no longer in office that doesn’t mean that we’re still not interested in accountability for all of your crimes and grift. We’re not going to forget,” he said at the time. “Like, we can’t forget about these folks that are causing harm, like, you know, I think it’s like, maybe it’s because I’m gay, but like, you know, like pettiness is a thing.”

Meanwhile, New York Magazine is detailing Garcia’s role in the future of targeting Trump officials, describing him as “part of the Democratic Party’s version of the Justice League.” He has already met with incoming House Intelligence Committee Chairman Jim Himes (D-CT) and Democrat Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-MS) — the likely head of the Homeland Security Committee — to discuss dividing up investigations into officials like former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and many, many more personalities.

However, Democrats are struggling to bridge the gap between their visceral desire to investigate Trump officials and their campaign promises to address affordability, the latter of which Americans are primarily focused on as wages fail to keep up with inflation.

Evidently, when Garcia is not thinking about investigations, he is thinking not of affordability but of “how to tell stories” on TikTok with the help of influencers. According to New York Magazine, “A quarter of his committee’s staff is dedicated to communications work: videographers, rapid response, flacks for new media (like influencers), and traditional press.”

“It’s much more like a presidential-style communication shop,” a staff director told the magazine. “No other committee on either side of the Capitol in either party has invested as much time and resources into communications”:

The staff has been thinking about how to package their work for an audience that would never watch a hearing on C-Span but might encounter a clip from one while scrolling through TikTok in bed. “We don’t want to be shouting into the darkness,” Edmonson says.
Garcia tells me he plans on communicating “everywhere,” whether that’s podcasts, Twitch streams, or mainstream media. He’s a regular on cable news and has even appeared on Bravo’s Watch What Happens Live With Andy Cohen, joking that he’d get to the bottom of some Real Housewives drama with a subpoena. (“Go get ’em,” Andy Cohen messaged him after the midterms.) “He’s been so good at getting attention,” says Rob Flaherty, a Democratic consultant who served as deputy campaign manager for both Joe Biden and Kamala Harris. And Flaherty is of the mind that, as long as the Democrats’ energy is focused, there really is no such thing as going overboard. “I do think more shots on goal is great,” he tells me. “You never know what’s going to break out.”

Garcia came under fire earlier this month after a failed attempt at humor on social media, comparing himself to Pennywise, the fictional, murderous clown character who targets and terrorizes children in Stephen King’s horror novel It, to showcase how “low” he is willing to go against his Republican opponents.

news.title: Biden accuses Pelosi of working 'furiously' behind scenes to derail his 2024 campaign
news.text: Former President Joe Biden wrote in his new book published Tuesday that former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi worked "furiously" behind the scenes to get elected officials and Biden delegates to abandon him in 2024, though Pelosi has denied leading a pressure campaign. "That same morning, after an appearance on Morning Joe, Nancy Pelosi came to see me privately in the White House. She had been a great friend through the years. I admired her skill as Speaker and as a legislative leader. I always saw her as the political operator who learned the trade from her father, Tommy D'Alesandro, the former mayor of Baltimore, as opposed to the wealthy, liberal San Francisco Democrat caricatured in the Republican attack machine," Biden wrote. Pelosi, in July 2024, following Biden's disastrous debate performance, said during an interview on "Morning Joe," "It’s up to the president to decide if he is going to run." The remarks suggested Biden was still weighing his options despite his insisting at the time he would remain in the race. HILLARY CLINTON HAMMERS JOE BIDEN FOR 2024 REELECTION BID DESPITE SUPPORTING CAMPAIGN: 'TERRIBLE MISTAKE' "Now, she was making a 'strategic reassessment.' Publicly she was still saying it was my decision to make. But privately she was working furiously behind the scenes to get elected officials and Biden delegates to defect," the former president wrote of Pelosi. Biden's book, "Promise Me, America," was published Tuesday and details his decision to exit the 2024 presidential race, as well as his decision to seek a second term, among other topics. JOE BIDEN SAYS CANCER SLOWED HIM DOWN, LIMITING MEMOIR PROMOTION TOUR The former president said Pelosi had heaped praise on him during their July 2024 meeting but sounded the alarm on the polling. "Then she told me how terrible my polling was and that I would be dragging her most vulnerable members down. She told me all the polling she had seen said I couldn't win, but I could be the George Washington of our time if I passed the torch," he wrote. EX-BIDEN STAFFER BLAMES BIDEN'S 'HUBRIS' FOR THE 'HELLSCAPE THAT WE LIVE IN': REPORT Biden wrote that Pelosi asked him to call one of his senior advisors, Mike Donilon, to go over the polling. "I told her I trusted Mike. That he had been with me for forty years. And he had been right in 2016 and 2020 and 2022 when so many of the pollsters had gotten it wrong. Mike walked her through the numbers, making the case that the race was close and still winnable. She didn't buy any of it. She told me that I wasn't getting an honest assessment of where the race stood. She was blunt: There were no polls that said I had any chance to win," Biden wrote. JILL BIDEN ADMITS PRESIDENT BIDEN WOULD NOT HAVE BEEN ABLE TO SERVE ANOTHER FOUR YEARS Biden ultimately dropped out of the race on July 21, 2024. He maintained in his book that he believed he was the best person to run against President Donald Trump, who defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris after she replaced Biden at the top of the Democratic ticket. Pelosi denied leading a pressure campaign in interviews following Biden's decision. JILL BIDEN REVEALS JOE WHISPERED 'I REALLY F---ED UP' AFTER DISASTROUS DEBATE WITH TRUMP During a "60 Minutes" interview in August 2024, Lesley Stahl told Pelosi that it had been reported Biden was "furious" with her. "I understand that you don't want to own this. But it is so well-reported that you were the leader of a pressure campaign," Stahl said. "No, I wasn't a leader of any pressure party. Well, let me say things that I didn't do. I didn't call one person. I did not call one person. I could always say to him, 'I never called anybody.' What I'm saying is, I had confidence that the president would make the proper choice for our country, whatever that would be, and I said that. 'Whatever that is, we'll go with,'" Pelosi responded. During a December 2025 interview, USA Today's Susan Page asked Pelosi about the role she played in getting Biden to exit the race and whether she had spoken to him since. JOE BIDEN ADDRESSES CRITICS WHO SAID HE HID HIS STAGE 4 CANCER DIAGNOSIS IN UPCOMING MEMOIR "No, but I want to just recharacterize what you said. My conversations with the president were more about let's make sure we're understanding what the polls say, and there are certain attitudes that the public had, had they been taken into consideration. If they had sat down with more pollsters, it might have come to a place where we said, ‘This is it, the president should go,’ but they just decided that their polls were right and that was that. So I didn't go in there to say to the president, 'You shouldn't run.' I said, ‘We've got to compare polls because we have different numbers,'" Pelosi said at the time. Pelosi's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Biden listed the many people he called after he announced his exit. The list included Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., former President Bill Clinton, Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and several other Democratic governors, senators and representatives, as well as union leaders. Pelosi was notably absent from the list. However, the former president said there were many others he wished he could have called. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Near the end of Biden's book, he wrote that he reunited with Pelosi at an Italian restaurant in early 2026, noting that she had made clear where she stood on his re-election effort. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "While I had seen Nancy and her family briefly at a couple of previous events, our last real conversation had been the one in which she told me that it was my decision whether to continue my run for president, making it clear what her decision was. We didn’t discuss that episode. But we had been through too much together to allow a rift to go un-mended. And so we talked about life and family and politics and fell into the old rhythms of friendship. And I’m glad we did," he wrote.

news.title: Can Vance Reset Anti-Fraud Push?
news.text:
President Trump’s decision to remove JD Vance from negotiations with Iran may be raising questions about the vice president’s political future, but some good government groups are hailing Trump’s decision to have Vance focus on his position as “fraud czar.” 

Trump has made cracking down on waste and abuse one of his signature policies. But the administration’s anti-fraud efforts – including the Department of Government Efficiency, created in 2025, and the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, established in March – have been marked by poorly executed directives and difficult-to-verify claims. 

“It definitely hasn’t been front and center to this point, and instead more a matter of scattered press conferences and an agency here and there with something,” said Matt Weidinger of the American Enterprise Institute.

Government watchdog groups hope that Vance’s streamlined portfolio will provide a necessary reset for what they see as long-overdue policy changes. They also note that it is easier to assail fraud, waste, and abuse than to root it out. Fraud in federal programs has remained a thorny problem for decades, raging on despite scattershot efforts to combat it from inspectors general, congressional committees, and the like. The same is true for waste, which usually takes the form of improper government payments. 

The Government Accountability Office estimates that the federal government loses between $233 billion and $521 billion annually to fraud, based on data from fiscal years 2018 through 2022. Improper payments – especially overpayments – are another persistent problem, though they are not necessarily fraudulent. Agencies reported an estimated $186 billion in improper payments in fiscal 2025.

Recovery efforts recoup only a fraction of those losses, experts told RealClearInvestigations. They cited the expense of prosecuting smaller cases, the difficulty of recovering money from perpetrators who flee or move assets, and limited coordination among federal agencies and law enforcement authorities. The government is also loath to dun citizens for overpayments they received through little or no fault of their own.

To change this, Trump is adopting a whole-of-government approach that, if successful, might burnish Vance’s political prospects following bruising midterm defeats. Failure, on the other hand, could saddle a potential Vance campaign as Kamala Harris was by her ineffective stint as the Biden administration’s “border czar.”

“At a minimum, the task force is a good idea because it puts fraud in the public conversation and shows the president is taking it seriously,” said Jeremy Portnoy, an investigator with the non-profit OpenTheBooks, which seeks transparency in all government spending. “Trump certainly talks about fraud more than most other presidents and that in itself is a positive.”

For now, it remains unclear whether Vance’s role will yield measurable results or political benefits. “So far it hasn’t been the albatross some predicted for Vance, and if it succeeded it could still be to his credit,” Weidinger told RCI.

Big guns, scattered shots

Trump has rolled out some of his biggest guns to battle fraud, waste, and abuse – creating the Elon Musk-led DOGE in 2025, and then tapping Vance last spring to head the anti-fraud effort.

But the task force, composed of representatives of every Cabinet-level department except the Department of Defense, along with some agencies with fraud issues such as the Small Business Administration, was bogged down by both political opposition from Democrats and its own inefficiency.

Trump’s executive order creating the task force last March gave departments and agencies 30-day and 60-day deadlines to submit “descriptions of such transactions and processes and suggested measures to prevent such fraud,” and directed the task force itself “to adopt, as appropriate, minimum anti-fraud requirements for transactions and processes.”

Trump administration officials told RCI that all the deadlines had been met. However, some six months after their latest due dates, none of the plans are available for public review.

The lack of public plans makes it difficult to assess the task force’s progress, Weidinger and others said. By way of comparison, when President Biden requested a “whole of government” approach to diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives, the bureaucracy appeared to respond with alacrity, and something similar should have happened via the Anti-Fraud Task Force, they said.

“If the government is doing something, they should be telling the people,” said Tom Schatz, president of Citizens Against Government Waste. “That’s what you would normally do running a business.”

In addition to a lack of transparency, the administration’s anti-fraud efforts have been bedeviled by fuzzy math. In June, for example, Education Secretary Linda McMahon said, “Our efforts prevented more than $1 billion in student aid fraud,” after the House passed a bill to fight back against “ghost students” getting federal loans.

“But no one could give us any data or the math on that,” Portnoy said. “I can’t say it isn’t true, just that no one has been able to substantiate it.”

Similarly, after the House Committee on Energy and Commerce released a report on Medicaid and Medicare fraud weeks before the midterms, it featured a pull quote from Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. saying that the Biden administration had cut program oversight to the bone while spending was skyrocketing to some $2.2 trillion per year.

“Yeah, I mean the most shocking thing to me was the Biden administration opening the door to waste, fraud, and abuse,” Kennedy testified in April. “We had a program integrity office. There were 80 people in it, which was not enough to cover 50 states and three territories. They fired immediately all but six of them. So we have no program integrity department.”

Neither the House committee nor the Department of Health and Human Services, however, could back up the secretary’s assertion in response to RCI’s questions. A spokesperson for CMS did not provide an answer to RCI’s question about Kennedy’s reference but insisted “program integrity remains a core priority.” A committee spokesperson said they could not vouch for Kennedy’s figures.

The website for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services still lists a “Center for Program Integrity,” with a director, an annual budget of $1 billion and more than 500 employees. The Center’s principal deputy, Jeneen Iwugo, did not respond to RCI’s request for comment on whether the office had been shorthanded for a time, or if its oversight duties have been transferred elsewhere in the department. 

Nevertheless, fraud experts said the Biden administration had relaxed some oversight requirements, while emphasizing that the Trump administration had not substantiated its numerical claims. 

“There’s a lot of evidence the Biden administration pulled back on oversight, that it relaxed guardrails, paused eligibility checks and the like,” said Jeremy Nighohossian, a senior fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute who focuses on healthcare. “But a lot of the time the Trump administration can’t back up any of the numbers it gives, and there doesn’t seem to be any substantiation.”

More fuzzy math

The sketchy math claims extend to other calculations. The task force maintains the Fraud Ledger, which presents the administration’s claimed anti-fraud accomplishments. As of Nov. 17, the Ledger claims $391.6 billion in fraud that has been “uncovered,” “stopped,” or “enforced,” though again that total includes the 13 months before the Task Force formed. And projections on what fraud might be prevented have a ring like the “jobs saved” statistic invented by the Obama administration, and not everyone is convinced all the numbers are real. “Lots of estimates of fraud are just that – estimates that are never formally established,” Weidinger said.

Fraud “stopped,” for example, counts $72 billion “saved annually through administrative actions such as provider suspensions and rule changes.” In other words, that’s a projected figure – a highly subjective one at that – and because the Task Force is an executive creation and many of the Trump administration’s proposals were not codified, a future Democratic administration could end them.

Other media outlets have exposed weaknesses in the ledger, and since DOGE began its work in 2025, some have found an inability to back up all its figures independently. And the ledger doesn’t always move in the direction one might expect, which would be for the figures for fraud to grow in all three categories. On Sept. 27, for instance, The New York Times ran what it called a “fact check” on the ledger and at that point its total for “enforced,” meaning “indictments, settlements and financial fines,” was at $59.1 billion. Yet on Nov. 17, that total had fallen to $58.9 billion, indicating something went awry with previous estimates.

The case of the Small Business Administration also illustrates the problems with nailing down amounts of fraud. The SBA inspector general had estimated that of the $1.2 trillion it distributed as COVID relief via its Paycheck Protection Program and Economic Injury Disaster Loans, $200 billion was siphoned by fraudsters through fictional businesses, inflated payrolls, and the like. The Fraud Ledger, however, credits $146.8 billion in fraud across three categories to the SBA (which still gives it the biggest total of all departments and agencies listed).

Recovery blues

Another oddity is that no matter how precise the government’s figures are for detected or prosecuted fraud, the amounts recovered are always but a fraction of the total. Experts cited the increasing sophistication of foreign criminal organizations that target federal spending as a major obstacle to recovering stolen funds.

“In recent years, the number one reason has to be because the fraud was perpetrated by overseas criminal gangs and they didn’t wait around for the good guys to find out and try to recover it,” Weidinger said. “An estimated 70 percent of fraud involving pandemic unemployment benefits was due to overseas actors.”

Schatz noted that recovering that money is complicated for other reasons. In the case of COVID money, the statutes of limitations have expired in some cases, and an effort to extend them failed in Congress. Earlier, Congress cut the practice of Recovery Audit Contractors, who had some success in health care fraud recovery, after hospitals and other major employers complained to their elected representatives.

Since the Task Force launched, however, the administration has implemented some changes. CMS has reached out to its contractors to find “innovative ideas from the industry” to combat fraud. The agency has also made more of its data publicly available. This has unleashed a coterie of citizen sleuths, many of whom use powerful AI tools to scour the mountains of data.

Meanwhile, the SBA has opened new hotlines for reporting fraud. In May, the Justice Department unveiled data-driven “FOCUS” teams to root out fraud, and its National Fraud Detection Center launched in August.

Citizen sleuths

The results of these initiatives remain to be seen, and government officials are still sorting thinly sourced leads from legitimate targets in the flood of new information, some private investigators told RCI. Turning suggestions of fraud into cases that can be prosecuted is often time-consuming and expensive.

In addition, officials need to separate money lost through fraud from that lost by improper payments, which often go to hospitals and other legitimate businesses as well as individuals. Improper payments have cost taxpayers some $3 trillion since fiscal year 2003, and the $186 billion in improper payments the government made in FY2025 was an increase of $24 billion from the previous fiscal year, according to the GAO’s estimate.

In the end, experts say the most important work for the Task Force is wrenching the federal bureaucracy away from its usual patterns with fraud. Rather than “pay and chase,” where the government must first identify fraudulent activity in money spent and then spend more money chasing it, the programs need better checks to avoid spending the money in the first place.

White House officials acknowledged that, thus far, many of the anti-fraud measures are temporary, but said two factors, which could be slotted under “business as usual” in the Capitol, have worked against the Task Force from the outset.

One is a frustration with Congress, which has been reluctant to add anti-fraud measures to its spending bills. Nighohossian pointed to some legislative progress. He said last year’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” installed more frequent eligibility checks on Medicaid that “will be much harder for a Democratic administration to undo.” The House committee’s April report on fraud in Medicaid and Medicare did make 37 recommendations for how CMS could improve its efforts to combat fraud, all of which, the committee said, the Centers agreed with. In August, five months after Trump issued his anti-fraud executive order, Vance hosted a congressional “roundtable” event, but with the midterm results it seems highly unlikely the lame-duck Republican majority will make any moves before surrendering power in January.

A bigger problem than Congress, however, is the tremendous inertia built into the federal bureaucracy, according to several officials familiar with the Task Force’s work. For decades, they said, many federal agencies have operated on autopilot. The Trump administration is the first to set up a framework to address the problem seriously, according to Task Force officials. Finally, officials want agencies to work harder to prevent fraudulent payments rather than rely on “pay and chase” – detecting fraud after money has gone out and then trying to recover it. 

Much of the spending on major entitlements like Medicaid and Medicare, moreover, is administered by the states, which vary greatly in how seriously they care about fraud. Officials say the federal government must work more closely with them to implement stronger safeguards against fraudulent and improper payments.

“Medicaid services are not always designed with program integrity in mind,” the House report said, and “continue(d) reliance on reactive program integrity rather than preventive oversight” was one of the main culprits behind the tens of billions lost in fraud each year.

Schatz, who has been on Capitol Hill since 1986, said those are genuine issues. While flares go up from time to time when a scandal erupts, there has never been a comprehensive and sustained effort to change the way federal programs operate. If the Task Force accomplishes nothing more than a cooperative network to combat fraud between federal agencies, prosecutors, and state and local law enforcement, that would provide a lasting benefit.

Such a network would also show that Washington recognizes the need for sustained attention rather than responses driven by headlines, Schatz said. Because fraud harms taxpayers and intended beneficiaries, efforts to combat it should draw bipartisan support, he said.

“There seems to be a public acknowledgment that it’s OK to fix it,” he said. “It seems to me that should transcend administrations or whoever is in power in Congress.”

news.title: ‘Come on, fella’: Wyoming Republican governor-elect nominates Kamala-backing Democrat for AG, thumbing his nose at conservatives
news.text:
Wyoming Governor-elect Eric Barlow (R) has named three key leadership picks for his incoming administration. Barlow's choice of a dyed-in-the-wool Democrat to serve as attorney general has ruffled some feathers.

Barlow's nominee, Walter Eggers, is a Cheyenne-based energy sector lawyer who has been teaching in recent months at the University of Wyoming College of Law. He also happens to be a registered Democrat, and Federal Election Commission records show he has donated over $20,000 to Democratic campaigns and organizations in recent decades.

'Those people have proven their agenda of destroying everything that Wyoming has historically stood for.'

Eggers has, for example, donated to Harris for President; Biden for President; the Wyoming Democratic State Central Committee; the Democratic National Committee; Colorado Rep. Jason Crow's (D) 2018 campaign; and Hillary for America. He also donated to Obama for America eight times.

The longtime Democratic donor is keen to take the job should the Republican-controlled state Senate confirm him in the new year.

"I am, first and foremost, very grateful and honored by the governor-elect’s decision to appoint me to this position, subject to confirmation by the Senate," Eggers told Cowboy State Daily. "I am very interested in this job because I believe it will put me in a position to advocate for the state of Wyoming."

In the role, Eggers would be able to decide whether to continue current Attorney General Keith Kautz's work of defending the state's conservative legislation — including pro-life and reality-affirming laws — from liberal legal challenges.

RELATED: These Republicans are holding up Trump's judicial appointments 

 Bonnie Jo Mount/the Washington Post/Getty Images

"I would take on that representation and that obligation with the same zealous approach I’ve applied to all my representation in the past — and any representation I would conduct or oversee as attorney general," he told the Cowboy State Daily.

Wyoming state Rep. Chip Neiman (R) is among the conservatives who have spoken out about the Democrat's nomination.

"After promising us that he’d be a conservative governor, his first act before being sworn in is to elevate a democrat to Wyoming’s highest law enforcement office? Come on, fella," Neiman wrote in a recent op-ed. "Eggers’ nomination demands rejection by the Wyoming Senate."

Neiman underscored that Eggers has regularly donated to "the same Democrat movement that has engaged in lawfare against Wyoming’s core industries" and that has opposed protections for the unborn.

"A nominee whose campaign contributions align with the politicians who initiated and advanced the very litigation and rules Wyoming has fought against cannot be trusted in that role," added Neiman.

Republican state Sen. Laura Taliaferro is also concerned about whether a Democratic attorney general can be trusted.

"I think that anyone who donates to Democrats like Hillary, Obama and Biden is not someone who will look out for Wyoming’s best interests," Taliaferro said, according to the Open Range Record. "All of those people have proven their agenda of destroying everything that Wyoming has historically stood for."

Bob Ferguson, vice chairman of the Wyoming Republican Party, told the Open Range Record, "Based on Barlow’s record and everything he has supported and voted for throughout his career it doesn't surprise me a bit that he would put a dyed in the wool democrat in as the chief legal counsel and chief law enforcement office of the state."

Barlow has been classified as a moderate libertarian conservative by OnTheIssues and assigned a 41% lifetime "Freedom Score" on the John Birch Society's Freedom Index.

Neither Eggers nor the governor-elect's transition team immediately responded to Blaze News' requests for comment.

Not all Wyoming Republicans are worried about having a Democratic state attorney general.

"I wouldn’t think [party affiliation] would matter very much," state Sen. Charlie Scott (R) said, according to the Cowboy State Daily. "We’ve had in the past, attorneys general who were on the opposite party of the governor. They work for the governor, and they do what the governor says."

news.title: Biden Defends 2024 Run in New Memoir, Blames Media and Party Leaders for Debate Fallout
news.text:
Former President Joe Biden vigorously defends his decision to seek a second term in 2024 in his new memoir, published Tuesday, November 17 — a level of conviction he rarely displayed during the campaign itself. He also downplays the consequences of his disastrous televised debate performance, asserting that his critics could “never cite a single thing related to the presidency that I didn’t accomplish.”

HuffPost US obtained an advance copy of the 465-page book, titled Promise Me, America. Biden’s ongoing battle with prostate cancer limits his ability to promote the memoir.

The book reveals no regrets from the former president about his time in the White House — nor about his decision to run again at 82. “Some say I was deluding myself in thinking I could do this job at my age. My answer is simple: I was already doing the job,” he writes of his candidacy.

The final chapters, devoted to his decision to seek a new term, his withdrawal from the Democratic primary race and the defeat of former Vice President Kamala Harris — who succeeded him as the party’s nominee — paint a portrait of a man determined to answer his detractors.

Blame Placed on Media and Democratic Leaders

Biden dwells on his victories in the 2024 Democratic primaries, which faced little competition, and refuses to see them as mere confirmations of an inevitable outcome. He dismisses the idea that his age was a genuine obstacle to governing, framing it instead as a matter of appearance. He sought to overcome it with the help of Mitt Romney, then a Republican senator from Utah, who advised him to lengthen his stride in public.

According to Biden, perceptions of his debate performance were shaped more by the media and party officials than by his own difficulties speaking on stage. “The press and the pundits had decided my performance was disqualifying,” he writes, insisting that polls showed no decline in his candidacy against Donald Trump.

Internal Democratic Party polling at the time, however, indicated he risked losing several states traditionally favorable to his camp: Virginia, New Jersey, New Mexico, Maine and New Hampshire. He adds: “But the data wasn’t the point. The narrative was. And the narrative was bad. Everyone seemed to agree that I had lost. Worse still, everyone seemed convinced that nothing could be fixed.”

Bitterness Seeps Through the Pages

The image Biden has always cultivated — that of a jovial grandfather — steers him away from the virulent attacks another author might have unleashed in such a book. His bitterness nonetheless surfaces, both toward what he sees as the press’s lack of recognition for his record and toward what he considers the disloyal conduct of certain Democratic officials, including Nancy Pelosi and Chuck Schumer.

Recalling the NATO summit he hosted in the days following the debate, he notes that some articles focused more on a verbal slip — he had inadvertently called Kamala Harris “Vice President Trump” — than on the results achieved. “It was the perfect illustration of what was happening to me. The fact that I was leading a NATO stronger and more united than ever, and leading efforts to confront the worst aggression Europe had seen since World War II, didn’t matter. But confusing Harris and Trump? That was serious,” he writes.

Biden also invokes Donald Trump repeatedly to justify his own decisions, asserting that Americans could never have preferred Trumpist chaos to the stability of his leadership. The threat posed by Trump also explains, in his view, why he had no choice but to run: “I was the only one who had ever beaten Donald Trump,” he writes. “And I believed I was best positioned to beat him again.”

Democrats have largely distanced themselves from Biden, who left the White House with the lowest approval rating of any Democratic president in forty years, even as the party won both chambers of Congress in this year’s midterm elections. Many made no secret of their satisfaction that the publication of his memoir was postponed until after the vote.

news.title: Execs donate to mayor's campaign after no-bid contract
news.text:
Good morning, Chicago. ✶

🔎 Below: Mayor Brandon Johnson’s administration awarded a no-bid contract to a clout-heavy consortium to oversee O’Hare Airport’s “People Mover” transit system. Four officials connected to a Plainfield-based company that benefitted from that contract subsequently donated to Johnson’s campaign — an apparent violation of city ethics rules.

🗞️ Plus: A murder conviction is tossed after torture claims, Chaz Ebert carries Roger’s legacy while walking her own path and more news you need to know below.

📝 Keeping score: The Bulls fell to the Cavaliers, 126-115.

☀️ Today’s weather: Sunny with a high near 56.

📧 Subscribe: Get our morning newsletter delivered to your inbox weekday mornings.

⏱️: An 8-minute read

TODAY’S TOP STORY 🔎

Executives at firm with no-bid O’Hare deal donate to mayor’s campaign

Reporting by Robert Herguth

The contract: In July, Mayor Brandon Johnson’s administration awarded a no-bid contract worth up to $1 billion to a clout-heavy consortium to run and maintain O’Hare Airport’s automated transit system. The “People Mover” links parking lots, terminals and the airport’s rental car complex.

The donation: In October, four executives at Plainfield-based Harbour Contractors, Inc., each gave Friends of Brandon Johnson, the mayor’s campaign fund, $2,500, for a total of $10,000, records show.

The rule: In 2011, then-Mayor Rahm Emanuel signed an executive order banning City Hall contractors from giving campaign money to the mayor — a rule still in effect, meaning the Harbour donations appear to violate city ethics regulations.

Key context: Since Johnson’s 2023 election, the Sun-Times has reported on a number of instances where that prohibition was violated by his campaign, which then returned campaign money to donors. Johnson’s campaign said that’s what will happen here if it turns out it shouldn’t have taken the Harbour contributions.

In other news:

Review of city finances sought: Leaders of a renegade City Council coalition are seeking an independent review of the city’s finances to reassure Wall Street rating agencies after the resignationof Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch. Terminal 2 work starts: Construction has begun on a $917 million concourse at O’Hare’s Terminal 2, which will add natural lighting, wood details, interior greenery and, ultimately, 24 new gates. United Airlines outage: United said Monday it had resolved a technology issue that delayed departing flights, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop.

Murder conviction tossed amid torture claims involving police detective

Reporting by Chip Mitchell

Conviction tossed: A Cook County judge on Monday threw out the conviction of Anthony Garrett, 68, finding that his written confession in 7-year-old Dantrell Davis’ 1992 murder was likely tortured out of him.

The ruling: The judge’s written order made it clear she didn’t buy sworn testimony from Richard Zuley, 80, a retired Chicago detective accused of orchestrating Garrett’s alleged beating in custody after the fatal shooting. The judge ordered a retrial and Garrett’s transfer from an Illinois prison to Cook County Jail.

Key context: Davis was fatally shot as he walked to school with his mother in the former public housing complex Cabrini-Green. Garrett, convicted by a jury in 1994, was sentenced to 100 years in prison. Before his conviction was tossed Monday, Garrett’s attorney tied his alleged torture to Zuley-led coercion in a string of cases from 1987 to 2003 — including four murder convictions later thrown out.

Chaz Ebert carries Roger’s legacy – and walks her own path

news.title: In new memoir, Joe Biden blames son Hunter's felony conviction for 2024 debate flop
news.text: Former US President Joe Biden has blamed his son Hunter Biden’s felony convictions for affecting his mental state ahead of his disastrous June 2024 presidential debate against Donald Trump, saying the trial had taken an emotional toll on him.In his new memoir, Promise Me, America, released on Tuesday, Biden said he was already feeling unwell before the debate and had even undergone a Covid-19 test. However, he said his exhaustion was not the only thing weighing on him.“On June 11, my son Hunter had been convicted of three felonies in a federal courtroom in Wilmington, Delaware. And it was breaking my heart,” Biden wrote.According to the New York Post, which reviewed the memoir, Biden said the conviction had deeply affected him, coming just 16 days before his debate with Trump in Atlanta on June 27, 2024.A jury had found Hunter guilty of three federal gun charges, including lying about his drug use while purchasing a firearm and possessing a gun while using illegal drugs.Biden alleged that the prosecution was politically motivated and aimed at damaging his presidency.“It was obvious. Hunter was being raked over the coals because of me,” he wrote, adding that he feared Republicans would continue putting pressure on his son until they broke him.While Biden said the prosecution had failed to break Hunter, he admitted that it had taken an emotional toll on him.“But I would be lying if I didn’t admit that they took a piece out of me,” he wrote.The former president's latest explanation adds to the list of reasons previously offered by him and his allies for his stumbling performance during the debate. These included a cold, jet lag, exhaustion, his preparation schedule and sleeping pills.The debate raised fresh questions about Biden’s age and ability to continue as president. He eventually withdrew from the 2024 presidential race in July, clearing the way for then-Vice President Kamala Harris to become the Democratic nominee.Biden recalls ‘lowest moment’ during debateIn the memoir, Biden also revisited what he described as one of the lowest moments of the debate, when he gave a confusing answer while discussing the federal deficit.“I lost my train of thought, saw that my time was running out on the clock, and rushed the final part of my answer by blurting out: ‘We finally beat Medicare,’” he wrote.Biden said he had intended to say, “We finally beat Big Pharma”, referring to his administration’s efforts to negotiate lower prescription drug prices for Medicare recipients.He acknowledged that the moment became damaging to his campaign, despite referring to what he considered a major legislative achievement.“What should have been a highlight of the debate became Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job,” he wrote.Biden also defended his decision to seek a second term, arguing that the election remained winnable even after the debate. He said voters had concerns about inflation and immigration but insisted these were not insurmountable problems.The 480-page memoir also recounts his confrontation with Democratic Senator Joe Manchin over a $1.9 trillion Covid-19 relief package, as well as his recollection of a private note left by Trump when he departed the White House in January 2021.Biden further criticised Trump over his role in the January 6 Capitol riot, election denialism and pardons for those involved in the attack. He also defended his administration’s Afghanistan withdrawal and its handling of the economy.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

news.title: 'Greatest Failure of a President': Comedian Andrew Schulz Regrets Backing Donald Trump in a Scathing Rant
news.text: Comedian Andrew Schulz, who voted for Donald Trump in 2024 and interviewed him during the presidential campaign, has described the president's record as potentially the greatest failure of his lifetime. Schulz also accused Trump of abandoning key promises and alleged unprecedented corruption.Speaking on Saturday, 14 November, on The Brilliant Idiots, which he co-hosts with Charlamagne tha God, Schulz criticised the gap between Trump's campaign promises and his actions in office.The comments continue a public break with a president Schulz once supported. He had previously raised concerns about government spending and foreign policy.Andrew Schulz Questions Trump's Record'It's the greatest failure of a president of our lifetime, and—I don't know—ever, right?' Schulz said, according to Mediaite.He described what he saw as a sharp divide between Trump's campaign rhetoric and his actions in office. His central complaint was not only that promises had gone unfulfilled, but that the administration had pursued policies he believed contradicted them.Schulz also alleged levels of corruption and cronyism without precedent in Western democracy. That was his assessment; the podcast and the reporting on his comments did not independently establish the claim.In the remarks cited by Mediaite, Schulz did not identify specific contracts, appointments or court findings to support the breadth of his allegation.Trump appeared on Schulz's Flagrant podcast in October 2024, shortly before the presidential election. The interview, which lasted roughly 90 minutes, gave Trump an opportunity to speak to an audience beyond traditional political news programmes.Variety reported in July 2025 that the interview had attracted 9.6 million views on YouTube. The figure was reported at that time and should not be read as a current view count.Why Schulz Voted for TrumpSchulz later said his vote reflected frustration with Democrats, rather than an ideological conversion to conservatism.In a June 2025 interview with The New York Times, he described himself as a lifelong registered Democrat. He said he believed the party had denied its supporters a meaningful voice in the political process.He also criticised Kamala Harris's presidential campaign, arguing that its message offered too little change to Americans dissatisfied with the outgoing administration.Those comments help explain why Schulz's latest criticism focuses on expectations. He supported Trump partly because he wanted a departure from policies he associated with the political establishment. He has since questioned whether that change had taken place.Criticism Began in 2025Schulz had voiced concerns about Trump's record before the November remarks. During a July 2025 episode of Flagrant, he complained that Trump was supporting foreign conflicts and increasing spending instead of reducing government expenditure.'I voted for none of this,' he said at the time, according to Variety.Schulz also recalled receiving messages from people who challenged him over the administration's decisions. He argued that Trump's actions did not reflect the policies he believed he had supported at the ballot box.The latest comments continue that dispute over whether Trump's second term has delivered the changes that convinced Schulz to vote for him.Trump appeared on popular podcasts during the 2024 campaign, seeking to reach voters outside conventional political media. Schulz's criticism now puts his own earlier interview with Trump in a different context: he has moved from giving the candidate a lengthy platform to publicly questioning the president's record.
news.author: Maybelyn B. Paden

news.title: No more permanent coalitions: What the midterm results reveal
news.text:
ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once said. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”

In 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory. 

Or so we were told. 

Now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again? 

Or so we are told. 

A big takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics. 

What may have looked like a new GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies. 

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

Trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3. 

Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ new populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades. 

White evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion. 

What's next

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath. 

If you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican. 

In other words, things change. 

If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year. 

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty. 

At the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.
news.author: Nathan L. Gonzales

news.title: AOC Files for Reelection as Socialists Push Her to Run for President
news.text: Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has filed paperwork with the Federal Election Commission to run for New York’s 14th Congressional District in 2028, setting up a bid for a sixth term in the House. Supporters in the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter are urging her to run for president. The House filing signals that Ocasio-Cortez is registering her candidacy for that seat; by itself, it does not settle whether she will later pursue a presidential or Senate campaign. Ocasio-Cortez has represented parts of the Bronx and Queens since 2019, after defeating longtime Representative Joe Crowley in the 2018 Democratic primary. She has since become one of the party’s most-prominent progressive lawmakers and a leading figure in the national Democratic debate. Newsweek has reached out for comment from Ocasio-Cortez and NYC-DSA via email, outside office hours, and is awaiting responses. What Has AOC Said About a 2028 Presidential Run? Ocasio-Cortez has not announced a decision about her political plans for 2028. In September, she told The New York Times she expected to decide after the 2026 midterm elections whether to seek the presidency, challenge Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer or run for reelection to the House. Following the midterms, she still had not publicly declared which path she would take. "I’m not naive to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latin," Ocasio-Cortez said. "And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities." She has previously described her goal as changing the country, rather than simply seeking a particular title or seat. In an August appearance on ABC’s This Week, she said her focus was on the midterms and, when asked about a possible Senate bid, said "anything is possible at this juncture." Ocasio-Cortez's FEC filing comes amid reports that she is weighing her options and has recently made changes to her political team. Those moves have not been presented as confirmation that she has decided to run for president or the Senate. NYC-DSA Calls on AOC to Run for President At its November 14 convention, NYC-DSA passed a resolution titled "Run AOC 2028 To Win A Democratic Socialist President." The measure received 291 votes in favor and 123 against, according to City & State New York. The resolution urges Ocasio-Cortez to run and commits the chapter to building support for a potential campaign and is not a formal endorsement of a presidential candidacy. NYC-DSA Co-Chair Gustavo Gordillo said the group would work to create conditions for a campaign focused on a working-class political agenda. The chapter has backed Ocasio-Cortez in her previous House races. Its latest move adds to other efforts by progressive organizers to encourage her to enter the 2028 contest, including the Ready for AOC campaign. Ocasio-Cortez rejoined DSA in August after her membership had lapsed. What Polls and Prediction Markets Show In an Economist/YouGov survey conducted November 9 to 11, Ocasio-Cortez received 12 percent among respondents who said they would vote in a 2028 Democratic primary or caucus. She ranked fourth in the results, behind former Vice President Kamala Harris at 20 percent, Senator Jon Ossoff at 15 percent and California Governor Gavin Newsom at 13 percent. The question asked respondents to name their preferred candidate, rather than choose from a fixed list. On Polymarket, Ocasio-Cortez was at 15 percent in the Democratic presidential nominee market on November 17, behind Ossoff at 26 percent. These prices reflect traders’ positions and can shift with new information; they are not polling results or a formal forecast. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Daniel Orton and James Debens
news.summary: Ocasio-Cortez has filed to run for the House in 2028, while NYC-DSA is urging her to consider a presidential campaign
news.author: Faye James

news.title: New ‘Jon Ossoff for President’ Website Launches As His 2028 Chances Surge
news.text: Jon Ossoff is leading prediction markets on both the 2028 Democratic nomination and the presidency as supporters launch an unofficial website encouraging the Georgia senator to run. His ascent follows an 18-point reelection victory in a state President Donald Trump carried two years earlier, giving Democrats fresh evidence that he can win beyond the party’s safest territory. The movement puts a relatively unfamiliar lawmaker into an emerging national contest, although Ossoff has said he is not seeking the White House. Newsweek emailed Ossoff’s senatorial campaign on Tuesday morning for comment. Why It Matters Presidential speculation often focuses on name recognition, fundraising, and ideological appeal. Ossoff now offers something more concrete: a 59 percent-to-41 percent win over Republican Mike Collins in one of America’s most closely watched battlegrounds. That result has given traders and activists a reason to reassess a politician who began the campaign considerably behind better-known Democrats in early 2028 measures. Sponsored by Kalshi Key Points Supporters Build A Campaign-In-Waiting The Draft Ossoff website presents itself as an unofficial, volunteer-run effort that is not authorized by Ossoff or any candidate committee. “Ok hear us out,” the site's homepage reads. “Jon Ossoff for President.” “He says he’s not running,” it continues, before inviting visitors to join a list of people who would turn out if he changed his mind. Organizers highlight his two statewide victories, previous work making investigative films and connection to late Representative John Lewis, whose congressional office employed him when he was younger. The project says personal information will never be sold, while donations pass directly to the senator’s existing committee. That distinction matters. The operation demonstrates enthusiasm around Ossoff, but it is not evidence that he has assembled staff, authorized a presidential committee or reversed his public position. Sponsored by Kalshi Traders Reprice The Democratic Field At 3:30 a.m. ET on Tuesday, Kalshi gave Ossoff a 27 percent chance of becoming the Democratic nominee, up 12.7 percentage points since Election Day. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez followed at 14 percent, with California Governor Gavin Newsom on 10 percent. The platform’s market on the eventual White House winner placed the senator first on 18 percent, a gain of 7.5 points since November 3. Vice President JD Vance stood at 13 percent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio at 9.2 percent. Polymarket showed a similar ordering. Ossoff was priced at 26 percent for the nomination, 11 points higher than on midterm night, while his presidential contract stood at 21 percent after rising eight points. Those figures are snapshots of contracts bought and sold for money. They reflect collective expectations among participants, including beliefs about whether someone will enter the race, survive the primaries and prevail in the general election. They are not equivalent to the share of Americans planning to vote for that person. Polling Shows Promise And A Recognition Problem A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted from November 6 to 9 found 29 percent of registered Democrats considered Ossoff an “excellent” potential candidate. Buttigieg received the same rating, while Kamala Harris and Newsom each registered 23 percent. The nationwide survey covered 1,705 adults, including 538 registered Democrats and 477 registered Republicans. Party-level findings carried a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 5 percentage points. Respondents were assessing candidate quality rather than choosing whom they would support in a primary. More than one-third of Democrats had not heard of Ossoff or did not rate him, compared with roughly one-fifth for Buttigieg. Low familiarity is both an obstacle and an opening. Building recognition would consume money and time, but fewer voters have fixed opinions about the Georgia senator than about several nationally established rivals. Georgia Provides His Strongest Argument Ossoff’s reelection offers a clearer political credential than any early contract or hypothetical survey. Winning by 18 points in a state Trump carried by two in 2024 allows supporters to present him as a Democrat capable of attracting voters outside the party’s national base. It also transforms his 2021 breakthrough from a narrow special-election success into evidence of a durable statewide coalition. Yet a presidential primary tests different skills. Potential contenders must organize across multiple states, withstand sustained scrutiny and persuade activists whose priorities may not resemble those of a general-election electorate in Georgia. What Happens Next No leading Democrat has formally entered the 2028 contest. For now, Ossoff has something short of a campaign but more substantial than idle speculation: activists gathering names, traders committing money and a landslide result beneath the argument that he could win. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Emma Lee-Sang
news.summary: Ossoff's decisive Georgia win elevates him in early 2028 markets and polls, as Democrats look toward their next White House race.

news.title: The Winning Democrat Who Wants to Break Up Political Parties
news.text:
This is an edited transcript of “The Ezra Klein Show.” You can listen to the episode wherever you get your podcasts.

One of the races I was following most closely across the election was Rob Sand’s race for governor in Iowa. Last time a Democrat won the Iowa governor’s mansion was 2006, when Chet Culver took it. It’s one of the states Democrats used to be very, very competitive in but then seemed to have lost almost entirely.

Sand was running a race that was distinct from everything else I saw across the country this year. He’s a Democrat who ran as a Democrat, but his big pitch was that he wanted to destroy the two-party system.

Archival clip of Rob Sand: That is what we mean on the yard signs and the T-shirts when we say it’s time to make Iowa not redder or bluer, just better and truer.

He wanted to end the two-party duopoly — what he liked to call the private clubs — in Iowa. And man, did it work.

Sand won the governor’s mansion in Iowa not by a little but by a lot. He won it by 11 points — far better than both how Kamala Harris fared in the state in 2024, and how the Democrat for governor did in 2022.
news.summary: Iowa’s governor-elect, Rob Sand, ran on a platform criticizing the two-party system. How will he translate his campaign message into reform?
