news.title: The Root Class of 2026: Meet The People Who Shaped The Year
news.text:
The Root 100 Class of 2026 has officially been unveiled, and this year’s group of culture creators are the ones to watch! Not only do they shape what we watch, wear, and aspire to—they’re the tastemakers leaving real influence and impact in the worlds of art, entertainment, sports, style, and media. 

Click here to check out the rest of our annual Root 100 list and keep reading to see which of your faves were honored as one of this year’s culture creators!

Druski has turned his viral internet comedy into a full-fledged entertainment career, using his hilarious character work to poke fun at everything from megachurch culture to the music industry. In 2026, he made history as the youngest host of the BET Awards and the first digital-native creator to host “Saturday Night Live”—the latter of which brought the long-running sketch show its highest viewership in two years! Next, we’ll see how he translates his comedic skits to the small screen thanks to his forthcoming Netflix church series.

Related: The Root 100 · Class of 2026

Jaafar Jackson

Jaafar Jackson successfully did the unthinkable, bringing his uncle Michael Jackson’s legacy to life in his screen debut, “Michael,” with show-stopping precision and an uncanny resemblance. His portrayal captured the King of Pop’s electrifying stage presence and softer side, helping propel the film to the biggest global opening for a music biopic ever and bringing in more than $1 billion at the worldwide box office. With part two of the biopic on its way, Jaafar is showcasing that he isn’t just carrying on a legendary family name—he’s making one of his own.

Kevin Fredericks, better known as KevOnStage, has turned his internet comedy success into a growing media empire. In 2026, he secured a multi-year partnership with Tubi, landed multiple series projects, launched “The Bald Brothers” podcast with Tony Baker, and co-hosted the 57th NAACP Image Awards Creative Arts ceremony. No matter what platform he’s on, KevOnStage stays showing creators what building and owning your own lane can look like!

Law Roach has cemented himself as one of fashion’s most influential forces, creating unforgettable looks for celebrities like Zendaya, Teyana Taylor, A$AP Rocky and Kerry Washington. Beyond the red carpet, the self-described “Image Architect” continues speaking out about fashion’s racial inequities, while making history as ASOS’ first-ever stylist in residence. He’s also passing his knowledge on to the next generation as a judge on “Project Runway,” serving style tips and shade all at the same time.

The New York Knicks Starting Five

The 2025–2026 New York Knicks made franchise history, bringing the city its first NBA championship since 1973. Led by Jalen Brunson, Karl-Anthony Towns, Mikal Bridges, Josh Hart and OG Anunoby, the team relied on chemistry, resilience and an undeniable sportsmanship throughout its historic season. Their championship run gave New Yorkers plenty to celebrate and reminded basketball fans what happens when a team truly plays for one another.

Wisdom Kaye

Wisdom Kaye has turned his fashion-forward social media videos into a global career, earning recognition as one of the internet’s most influential style stars. In September 2026, he received the Virgil Abloh Award from LVMH during Harlem’s Fashion Row’s annual Fashion Show & Style Awards, adding another major milestone to his résumé. With more than 14.6 million TikTok followers and consistent standout appearances at the Met Gala, Kaye continues to prove that digital creators belong at fashion’s biggest tables!

Dominique Morgan

Affectionately known as “The People’s Auntie,” Dominique Morgan has built a platform around offering wisdom, guidance, and support to underserved communities. Through her work as an award-winning artist, activist, and speaker, along with her Substack community of more than 500,000 subscribers, she tackles everything from faith and relationships to pop culture and politics. A recipient of the NAACP Freedom Fighter Award, Morgan continues using her voice to show up for the people who need her most, all while giving a loving rebuke or comedic message at the same time.

Durand Bernarr

Ever since he was a teen singing on YouTube, he’s been putting in work behind the microphone and achieving iconic feats like serving on the production side with his father with Earth, Wind & Fire’s tours years ago. After spending years singing background vocals for Erykah Badu, the Cleveland native finally struck out on his own and remained independent in an industry dominated by major labels. That bet on himself paid off when he won the 2026 Grammy for Best Progressive R&B Album (and became one of our favorite meme-providers thanks to his hilarious Grammys acceptance speech).

Ziwe has built her comedy career around asking the questions other people are too afraid to touch, turning uncomfortable conversations about race, privilege, and celebrity culture into hilarious, satirical content. With more than 697,000 YouTube subscribers and 357 million total views, she’s proving that fearless interviews and a little awkwardness make for very good entertainment.

Mojo Brookzz

Mojo Brookzz has turned his sharp and hilarious observations about Black culture into a thriving comedy career, building a massive social media following along the way. The Chicago native’s rise reached new heights in 2026 with his debut Netflix comedy special, “Mojo Brookzz: I Know You Lying,” and a starring role in Tyler Perry’s “Miss Governor.” Brookzz was also named one of Variety’s 10 Comics to Watch in 2025, proving that his unapologetic humor is on the rise.

Keke Palmer

Keke Palmer continuously proves there’s little she can’t do, expanding her reach across acting, television, fashion and digital media. Named to the Hollywood Walk of Fame’s Class of 2027, she’s keeping audiences entertained as the host of “Password” and through her hit podcast, “Baby, This Is Keke Palmer,” which has seen iconic guests like Oprah and former Vice President Kamala Harris. She’s also returning to scripted television in Peacock’s renewed series “The ‘Burbs,” which recently received a second season renewal, and starred in Boots Riley’s quirky film “I Love Boosters.”

With more than 17 million TikTok followers, Keith Lee has become one of the internet’s most influential food critics, using his platform to spotlight overlooked Black-owned and family-run restaurants. In 2026, he expanded that mission with his first FamiLee Day food and music festival in New Orleans, where participating food vendors didn’t have to pay to take part. He also showed up for Gary, Indiana, residents after a devastating storm, distributing thousands of meals and relief kits while donating $15,000.

Michelle Buteau

Michelle Buteau has never been one to stay in a single creative lane, and her hit Netflix series “Survival of the Thickest” is proof. As the show’s co-creator, writer, and star, she brought a refreshing story of self-love and reinvention to the screen while putting plus-size Black women at the center. She took things a step further in 2026, making her directorial debut during the show’s final season and showing that she’s just as comfortable calling the shots behind the camera.

Jennifer Hudson

As an EGOT winner, Jennifer Hudson has earned her place among entertainment’s most celebrated multi-hyphenates. Thanks to her eponymous daytime talk show, she’s become one of daytime television’s most beloved hosts, earning five Daytime Emmy nominations in 2026 alone, including Outstanding Daytime Talk Series Host. Never straying far from her musical roots, Hudson was also tapped to perform the National Anthem at the 2026 World Cup Final and blew it out of the water, as expected.

Imani Ellis

Imani Ellis turned a small gathering in her Harlem apartment into one of the biggest creative movements celebrating Black culture. Since founding CultureCon in 2016, she’s grown the event into the world’s largest creative homecoming for Black artists, entrepreneurs and cultural influencers. This year, she welcomed 12,000 attendees to Brooklyn’s Duggal Greenhouse for the event’s “Museum of Us” edition, creating the perfect space for Black creatives to connect, collaborate, and be celebrated year after year.

Gail Bean is having a major moment in 2026, taking on leading roles in FX and Hulu’s “The Drop: A Snowfall Saga” and the upcoming final season of STARZ’s “P-Valley.” Whether she’s commanding the screen as a leading lady or bringing complex characters to life, it’s clear Bean has the range to make her one to watch. In addition to acting, she founded Dream Above The Influence, a nonprofit providing mentorship and resources to young people and families in historically underserved communities.

J. Alphonse Nicholson

Since breaking out as Lil’ Murda on Starz’s “P-Valley,” J. Alphonse Nicholson has become an audience favorite, earning praise for his authenticity and emotional range. In 2026, he continued building his résumé with a critically praised performance in “If I Go Will They Miss Me” and a role in HBO’s “Lanterns.” From his days as a New York street drummer to his growing Hollywood career, Nicholson continues to give audiences plenty of reasons to root for him.

André White Jr.

André White Jr. is making sure the Black stories left out of history books get the attention they deserve. Through his podcast, “Redacted History,” the educator and historian spotlights overlooked Black history and movements, earning the show Best DIY Podcast honors at the 2026 Ambies. A co-founder of the Aaron J. White Foundation with a doctorate in education from the University of Dayton, White makes history accessible for a new generation.

Conscious Lee

Conscious Lee (legally George Lee Jr.) has built an audience of more than 3 million followers by making history, politics, and culture accessible through impressive storytelling and his mantra: “Education is Elevation.” A former college educator with two master’s degrees, he brings his academic background to digital content, his podcast and Substack, which all helped him to earn a 2026 NAACP Image Award nomination for Outstanding Digital Content Creator in the Political/Culture category.

Erin Jackson

In 2026, Erin Jackson earned her third Olympic team selection and was chosen by her teammates to carry Team USA’s flag at the Milano Cortina Opening Ceremony. That honor came just four short years after she made history at the 2022 Winter Olympics in Beijing, becoming the first Black woman to win an individual Olympic gold medal. The Florida native then transitioned from inline skating to speed skating and quickly established herself as one of the sport’s best.

Emayatzi Corinealdi

Emayatzy Corinealdi is no doubt one of television’s most compelling leading ladies, and every episode of Hulu’s “Reasonable Doubt” just shows that. As the brilliant yet complicated defense attorney Jax Stewart, Corinealdi consistently brings depth and nuance to the character while she navigates complicated cases and personal struggles. When Season 4 premiered, the series became Hulu’s No. 1 streaming show, and now that they’ve secured a season five renewal, you can expect to see Corinealdi bring it even more!

Frederick Richard

Frederick Richard talked his talk and backed it up, publicly predicting he’d win gold at the 2025 World Championships months before taking the floor. The 22-year-old gymnast, also known as “Frederick Flips,” delivered on that promise and captured his first global gold in the floor exercise. In a sport where young Black men continue to be underrepresented, Richard’s success shows that confidence and preparation can make history.

Elizabeth Booker Houston

Elizabeth Booker Houston is bringing law, politics and a healthy dose of snark to the digital space. Armed with degrees in law, public health and psychology, the Memphis-based creator breaks down complicated policy issues for the everyman and her growing audience of more than 800,000 Instagram followers. In 2026, her influence earned her an NAACP Image Award nomination for Outstanding Digital Content Creator in the Political/Culture category.

 J. Bolin has been in the fashion game for almost 20 years, styling celebrities like Brandy, Morris Chestnut, and more. But in June 2026, he launched House of Bolin, merging his expertise in fashion, interior design, and event production all under one new venture. Talk about not being limited to just one creative outlet!

Kara Lawson

Kara Lawson has gone from standout basketball player to one of the most respected coaches in the women’s game, inspiring athletes along the way with her “Handle Hard Better” philosophy. In 2026, she led Duke to both the ACC regular-season and tournament championships, earning the conference’s Coach of the Year honors, while also guiding the U.S. Women’s National Team to a world championship. Drawing on her experience as an elite player and leader, Lawson is showing all of us how to build a winning foundation for the next generation of women in sports.

Mike Brown brought a new winning era to the New York Knicks, leading the franchise to its historic 2026 NBA championship in his debut season. The team finished the regular season with a 53-29 record, won the 2025-26 NBA Cup and carried that momentum into a dominant playoff run. After over 50 years of waiting, Knicks fans finally have another championship to celebrate, thanks in part to Brown’s experience and leadership.

Nneka Ogwumike

Nneka Ogwumike has spent 15 years making her mark on the basketball court while fighting to make the game better for women athletes. As the Women’s National Basketball Players Association president, she helped secure a historic 2026 collective bargaining agreement that included a 53% increase in average total compensation, a $7 million salary cap, and expanded maternity and family-planning benefits.

Sonja Norwood

Sonja Norwood is bringing forgotten Black American food traditions back to the table through her viral “Lost Black American Recipes” series. With more than 1.1 million Instagram followers and 1.4 million TikTok followers, she serves up recipes like burnt sugar cake and molasses pull candy alongside the history behind each dish. Her mix of food, cultural storytelling and unfiltered reactions has turned food history into must-watch content.

Sarah Lewis

As attacks on Black history continue through legislation and book bans, Harvard professor Sarah Lewis is making sure important stories aren’t forgotten. Her curated exhibition, “If Emmett Till Lived,” at the Museum of Contemporary Photography in Chicago features works from more than 110 artists imagining the life and future stolen from 14-year-old Emmett Till, who was lynched in Mississippi in 1955. Through art and historical reflection, Lewis is creating space to confront the past while honoring the possibilities that were taken away.

Laila Edwards

In 2026, Laila Edwards made history at the Winter Olympics as the first Black woman to play Olympic hockey for Team USA, helping lead the squad to gold with two goals and six assists. The Cleveland Heights native continued her winning streak by helping the University of Wisconsin capture its third NCAA national championship in four seasons before being selected fourth overall in the 2026 PWHL draft. With plenty of career left to go, Edwards has already made it clear she’s not interested in settling for anything less than greatness—and we’re here for it!

Taylor Townsend

Taylor Townsend has continued her rise in professional tennis, making major moves on the international circuit and adding to her Grand Slam legacy. In 2026, she and her doubles partner completed a career Grand Slam in Women’s Doubles, capturing both the French Open and U.S. Open titles. At this point, the former world No. 1 junior has officially established herself among the sport’s elite, proving she’s a force to be reckoned with.

Trinity Rodman

Trinity Rodman made major moves in 2026, signing a reported $2 million-a-year contract with the Washington Spirit to become the highest-paid player in women’s soccer and the first player to captain the U.S. women’s national team just two days after signing. Her landmark deal also helped inspire a new NWSL salary rule. Fresh off an impressive playoff run that helped send Washington to the championship, the Olympic gold medalist is showing she’s only getting started.

Elana Meyers Taylor

After years of coming close, Elana Meyers Taylor finally captured individual Olympic gold at the 2026 Winter Games in Cortina d’Ampezzo, Italy. The 41-year-old mother of two made history as the oldest woman to win an individual Winter Olympic gold medal, while tying Bonnie Blair for the most Winter Olympic medals by an American woman. With six medals to her name, she also extended her record as the most decorated Black athlete in Winter Olympic history. That’s what it looks like to never give up on your dreams, folks!

news.title: Senate leadership challenge presents fork in the road for Democrats
news.text:
As the euphoria of the midterm election success begins to fade for the Democratic Party, so comes the first true test of their resolve, direction and identity. 

Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland senator whose mild disposition belies an outspoken progressive streak, is adamant that he can muster the votes to topple Chuck Schumer as the incumbent US Senate majority leader. 

‘Repudiation’ became the overnight commentariat buzzword of the midterms. Van Hollen’s argument is that the Senate blindly persisting with the status quo – in the familiar face of Schumer – would be akin to a repudiation of the wishes of the American voters.

“I think this is a wide-open race, and I think the American people spoke loudly and clearly on election day,” he said this week.

“First of all, they rejected Trump’s policies – his wars, corruption, the high costs. But they haven’t fully hired the Democrats. We have a chance, but we need to earn people’s trust. So, this isn’t about any one individual. It is about what the American people had to say.”

Van Hollen’s challenge has sharpened the contrast between the progressive and establishment wings of the party. A host of new senators – including the high-profile Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, Adam Hamilton of Kansas and Troy Jackson, who ended Susan Collins’s 30-year run in Maine – have all stated their intention not to vote for Schumer. 

Others, such as Angus King, the Maine Independent who caucuses with the Democrats, are arguing that Schumer is the architect of the historic sweep that has led to the party winning some 55 Senate seats – a figure predicted by precisely nobody. “Why would you fire the manager who just won the World Series?” he pointed out.

Schumer himself has been publicly relaxed about Van Hollen’s challenge, stating last week he is confident he has the votes (in a straight majority election count) and that he welcomes debate. The 75-year-old New Yorker has been a fixture in the Senate since 1999, adopting a smiling and avuncular political manner as he assumed godfather status within the party. 

Irish lobbyists will recall him as a staunch supporter of the immigration Bill, originally co-authored by Patrick Leahy, the influential Vermont senator, and Dick Durbin of Illinois, that would have granted some 10,000 undocumented Irish a path to attain legal status under the proposed E-3 non-immigrant visa. The Bill was introduced by Schumer in 2012 but did not pass. 

Schumer has remained a trenchant defender of US support for Israel, even if one of his more outspoken moments lay in his criticism of Binyamin Netanyahu, whom, he told the chamber in March of 2024, had “totally lost his way” in his leadership of a government that “no longer fits the needs of Israel”. 

The words were stronger than anything offered by president Joe Biden as the onslaught against Gaza worsened. But Schumer has a long-standing relationship with AIPAC, the biggest pro-Israel lobbying group, while Van Hollen has referred to Netanyahu as a “chronic liar” and a “wanted war criminal” and has actively worked to halt arms shipments and military aid to Israel.

To the new generation, that sharp contrast leaves Schumer out of step: a member of the Biden-era vanguard and not representative of the fervent wish for economic and social reform as expressed in election results that upended historical precedent in states such as Iowa and Texas. 

Van Hollen has also suggested that behind the scenes, Schumer is lobbying to bring forward the election debate from December 1st before his challenge can fully catch fire.

“I think there is an overwhelming sentiment that we should have a fair and open process,” he told Politico on Monday in one of a series of interviews he has given in recent days.

“After all, we called for a fair and open process in the national elections, and it would be kind of strange if the Democratic Party cut short debate and used that to influence the outcome of the election. I would just ask why that would be – that folks would want to cut debate short ... is it that the longer this discussion goes on, the more momentum grows?”

Contained within that rhetorical question is a haunting muscle-memory for the Democratic movement. The July 2024 decision by Biden to abandon his re-election bid was quickly alchemised into an August coronation, at the convention in Chicago, of then vice-president Kamala Harris. There were extenuating circumstances – not least that the election was three months out – and the Democrats enjoyed a late summer jolt of optimism about a presidential campaign that had flatlined following Biden’s catastrophic debate performance in Atlanta.

But the lack of process – and even a cursory debate about holding a primary so other candidates could make their case – plagued the party after Donald Trump returned to the White House. Trump could goad the Democrats about their decision to essentially replace Biden, who had been chosen by the public in the Democratic primaries – and goad them he did.

The stunning New York mayoral campaign by Democratic socialist candidate Zohran Mamdani last year presaged the wave of midterm campaigns. Last September, Van Hollen criticised Schumer and House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries for their reluctance to endorse their fellow New Yorker.

“That kind of spineless politics is what people are sick of,” he said in a speech in Des Moines.

“They need to get behind him and get behind him now.”

During the first six rampaging months of Trump II, the idea of the Democratic Party concocting the biggest midterm sweep in half a century would have seemed delusional. In all polls, the party was mired in dismal approval ratings and appeared clueless as to how to get out of that rut.

Against those odds, and through a combination of general disillusionment with the Iran war and other Trump policies, they have done so. Schumer supporters are adamant that he set the campaign manifesto of talking about cost, corruption and chaos – and chose key candidates such as Roy Cooper (North Carolina) and Sherrod Brown (Ohio). 

“Let’s be real,” Van Hollen argued this week.

“This was not a Washington-orchestrated election around the country. This was the American people wising up against a lawless president and demanding change. We won not just Senate seats and House seats, we won governor’s races, we won legislative races and if you look at some of the races we won say in Mississippi – Scott Colom wasn’t recruited by anybody in Washington. [Nor was] Annie Andrews in South Carolina.”

Not only that, but Schumer had actively supported Haley Stevens, the Michigan establishment pick narrowly defeated by El-Sayed in their primary election. Stevens’s tense relationship with El-Sayed broke down on the eve of the midterms, causing her to publicly endorse Republican candidate Mike Rogers, a stunning reversal that Schumer denounced as a “despicable betrayal”.

Among the sitting senators firmly in Schumer’s camp is John Fetterman, the Pennsylvania Democrat senator who has remained a staunchly pro-Israel advocate and has become increasingly estranged from the party mandate. Fetterman has said the prospect of Van Hollen leading the caucus could be a “red-flag” issue for him: there is a strong possibility that if Van Hollen does succeed in toppling the veteran, it could result in an immediate defection.

Many Democratic voters will see this leadership tussle as a referendum on the party’s internal ideological arm-wrestle. Its senators, returning and new, are going to have to make their decision by December 1st – if not before. It will represent their first real test after the November dream and there is no easy answer.

As Yogi Berra, the legendary New Yorker who knew a thing or two about winning and losing World Series said: “When you come to a fork in the road, take it.”
news.summary: Progressive senator Chris Van Hollen’s bid to topple establishment figure Chuck Schumer represents an ideological struggle within the party

news.title: Oversight chair James Comer enters Kentucky governor's race
news.text:
James Comer, the Kentucky Republican who chairs the House Oversight Committee, announced Monday night that he is running for governor in 2027, seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear.

Comer made his announcement during a tele-town hall. He is the first high-profile Republican to enter the race, NBC News reported. Beshear has governed Kentucky since 2019.

For most of the event, Comer took callers’ questions about education, small business and high prices. He said eliminating Kentucky’s income tax would be his top priority as governor.

“Kentucky needs a leader whose policies will lead to growth and good-paying jobs. We need a leader whose priority will be to reduce taxes so Kentuckians can keep more of what they earn,” Comer said.

Kentucky Democratic Party Chair Colmon Elridge criticized Comer’s Washington record in a statement, saying he advanced President Donald Trump’s agenda by “supporting the largest cuts to Medicaid and SNAP in American history while doing nothing to protect Kentuckians from Trump’s costly tariffs and chaotic war in Iran.”

“Very few candidates would have the confidence to run for governor on a record like that, but Jamie Comer has never been one to let facts get in the way of a good story,” Elridge said.

Comer addressed Trump’s national policies when a caller asked a question. “I think that some of the things the president has tried to do on the national level had good intentions, but there are always unintended consequences,” he said.

“Serving this state is a calling for me,” Comer said. He added, “The government doesn’t have all the answers, but we have a responsibility to solve problems and lift people up when we can.”

His campaign launch followed this month’s midterm elections, when Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress, NBC News reported. Trump carried Kentucky by roughly 30 points over Kamala Harris in 2024, according to Fox News.

U.S. Sen. Rand Paul endorsed Comer on X minutes after the announcement video went live.

I’m proud to endorse my friend @JamesComer to be Kentucky’s next Governor! Please help him to get there!— Rand Paul (@RandPaul) November 17, 2026

Agriculture Commissioner Jonathan Shell called into the livestream to endorse Comer. Secretary of State Michael Adams, Attorney General Russell Coleman and Rep. Brett Guthrie had pledged support for a Comer bid in August and on Nov. 2.

The Washington Examiner reported that Comer enters the Republican primary as the front-runner. He had spent months teasing a run and had indicated he would launch it shortly after the midterms.

Three other Republicans have indicated in Kentucky Registry of Election Finance filings that they plan to run. They are Rick Hardin of Leitchfield, Brett St. Amand of Lexington and Charles “Bruiser” Martin of London. Hardin is a state attorney, while Martin is a former reality TV contestant.

Two Democrats are running. Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman has served throughout Beshear’s tenure. Rocky Adkins, a longtime former state House leader, was Beshear’s senior adviser for more than six years.

Comer, 54, grew up in Tompkinsville, Kentucky, and graduated from Western Kentucky University. He served in the Kentucky House from 2001 to 2011, then spent one four-year term as state agriculture commissioner.

He has represented Kentucky’s 1st Congressional District since November 2016, when he won a special election to replace Rep. Ed Whitfield, who resigned. Comer has chaired Oversight since Republicans regained the House majority in 2023. Fox News reported that his investigations included the federal government’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein case and former President Joe Biden’s use of an autopen.

It was not immediately known whether Comer will retain his House seat and committee chairmanship during the campaign.

Kentucky’s primary elections are scheduled for May 18, followed by the general election on Nov. 2.

news.title: How a Black Democrat Survived Redistricting in Alabama
news.text:
Warren Tidwell is glad the election is over. 

Tidwell, a community organizer, recognizes there was a sea change on election night. 

“They say it was a blue wave,” Tidwell said. “Or a blue tsunami.”

But he’s tired of the water metaphors. 

For weeks, Tidwell had been working to help organize disaster relief across the rural Alabama counties that stretch atop the Florida panhandle. Because of the rains and winds of Hurricane Isaias, which hit Alabama last month, he’s seen enough water damage for a lifetime. So for him, the analogies fall flat. 

And for the residents he’s been helping, the election wasn’t a political game, he said. It was a cry for help. 

In Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, which includes many of the impacted counties, voters bucked state Republicans’ attempt to oust U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, a Black Democratic incumbent they had drawn out of his own district earlier this year. That move came after President Donald Trump called for redistricting in red states, and the Supreme Court ruled that the Voting Rights Act does not require the creation of majority-minority congressional districts to facilitate the election of minority voters’ candidates of choice.

Figures, running in the new, heavily Republican district, outperformed all expectations, defeating his Trump-endorsed opponent, Rhett Marques, by more than 7 points. Had those new boundaries been in effect during the 2024 presidential election, Donald Trump would have beaten Kamala Harris by 15 points, 57 percent to 42 percent.

“Where is FEMA?”

On Oct. 9, Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Florida Gulf coast around 8:30 p.m. local time, cutting its way across the middle of Alabama, eventually killing nine people across three states and causing billions of dollars in damage. 

On Oct. 24, all of Alabama’s congressional delegation—Republicans and Democrats— signed a letter supporting Gov. Kay Ivey’s request to Trump for a major disaster declaration for 23 counties in the southern part of the state, including much of the second district. They have received no reply. 

Instead, on Oct. 27, Trump issued a major disaster declaration for the 15 Florida counties in the path of the storm. Escambia County, Florida, residents would benefit from a major disaster declaration; residents of neighboring Escambia County, Alabama, still have no word whether they will get help. 

Everywhere Tidwell has travelled across the impacted counties in south Alabama, residents still struggling to meet their basic needs have asked him the same question: “Where is FEMA?”

Tidwell, who serves as executive director of the Alabama Center for Rural Organizing and Systemic Solutions, said many voters likely had that question in mind on election day. But disaster relief shouldn’t be about political affiliation, he said. 

“If someone asks me who these people voted for, I’ll scream,” he said. “These people need help, not a campaign promise.”

Pastor Timothy Williams, a resident of the historically Black Shiloh community in Coffee County, said voters living in the district were already tired of high prices and low wages before the hurricane. In its wake, Williams said, neighbors have had to rely on each other, not the federal government, to recover from the storm. 

“We haven’t seen much of any federal response,” Williams said. “The hurricane split light poles. It took trees. It damaged people’s roofs.” 

Williams’ family evacuated to a local motel during the storm instead of hunkering down in their home, which has repeatedly faced flooding since a 2018 highway expansion. 

Andrea Eckelman, a political science professor at the University of Montevallo, Alabama’s public liberal arts college, said that issues like disaster relief can compel voters to the polls for a very good reason.

“That’s the point at which it all starts to feel personal,” Eckelman said. “You may be able to explain away high prices for a while, but you can’t explain away why the family whose home has been destroyed isn’t getting help.”

Sources familiar with Ivey and Trump’s relationship told Inside Climate News that Trump’s delayed decision on a major disaster declaration for Alabama in the wake of Isaias stems from his icy relationship with the state’s governor, which began with the denial of Trump’s request to hold a political rally in 2021 onboard the U.S.S. Alabama, a battleship docked in Mobile Bay. Ivey denied any involvement in the decision to reject Trump’s request at the time. 

In a statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis denied that Trump’s decisions regarding disaster relief are motivated by politics. 

“The President responds to each request for Federal assistance under the Stafford Act with great care and consideration, ensuring American tax dollars are used appropriately and efficiently by the states to supplement—not substitute, their obligation to respond to and recover from disasters,” Bis wrote. “There is no politicization to the President’s decisions on disaster relief.” 

In an interview Monday, Rep. Figures said that he hopes the president isn’t playing politics with disaster relief decisions but that he wouldn’t be surprised. 

“Nothing would surprise me with this president and how petty [the White House] can be in terms of decisions they make—even decisions as basic as getting disaster relief to impacted communities,” Figures said. 

Figures’ first speech on the House floor in 2025 urged federal relief for California in the wake of the state’s historic wildfires.

“I still don’t know that they’ve received adequate aid like they would have gotten under a normal presidency, Democrat or Republican,” he said. 

As he fed his fussy one-year-old—his “fourth and final” child—Figures told Inside Climate News that Alabama’s congressional delegation and Gov. Ivey have done everything they can to secure a major disaster declaration.

“One would think that we’d be able to get a response quickly and go ahead and get resources down to the people who actually need it, but unfortunately that hasn’t happened yet,” Figures said. “But we’re going to keep pushing.”

Figures said that those most heavily impacted by the storm in Alabama are in areas of his former district now represented by U.S. Rep. Terri Sewell, also a Democrat, and that regardless of district lines, all Alabamians deserve access to disaster relief regardless of their politics. 

“Some of these are very rural communities with high levels of poverty and not a lot of infrastructure and certainly not a lot of local resources to respond to a major disaster like this,” he said. “So we need federal aid. We need it in those communities, regardless of whether they’re in my district or not. Those communities still need the federal government to be there when they need them most.” 

There’s a lesson to be learned here, Figures said. People need help from their government regardless of what voting district they’ve been placed into for political reasons. And those decisions—politicans choosing voters instead of the other way around—can ultimately have unexpected consequences at the ballot box.

Steve Flowers, a veteran GOP political commentator and former state House member, said that in the end, Republicans will have to realize that redistricting ultimately backfired, even in Alabama. Instead of creating new safe seats for Republicans, the redistricting drove Black voters to the polls in areas of the state where turnout has lagged for decades. That had impacts on election results, he said. Alabama may not have experienced a blue tsunami. But it got wet.

“It was probably a bad idea for Republicans,” Flowers said, “And Figures benefited from the blue wave across the nation, too.” 

Flowers acknowledged that Republicans in the state had tried their best to boot Figures from Congress in the wake of a U.S. Supreme Court decision further diminishing the Voting Rights Act. 

“They wanted to destroy his district,” Flowers said of state Republicans. 

Instead of “destroying the district,” the GOP plan drove Black turnout. Figures won more votes in majority-Black Montgomery County in the midterm election than he had in the last presidential cycle. 

Alabama Republicans knew Shomari Figures is a Mobile man. 

His father, civil rights attorney Michael Figures, had helped bankrupt the Klan in the wake of the 1981 lynching of Michael Donald, a black teenager, in the state’s port city. His mother has represented Mobile in the state Senate for years, championing air quality reforms while cheering on her son, who worked at the U.S. Department of Justice before his tenure in Congress. 

So when the state GOP went to the drawing board, they knew what they were doing, Flowers said. State Republicans, emboldened by the national push to redistrict, placed Figures in a district that didn’t include Mobile, his hometown and incorporated areas of the predominantly white Wiregrass in the far southeastern part of the state. 

“I don’t think it’s a secret,” Figures said Monday. “They were hoping to get rid of me and then probably take steps in the next session to try and get rid of [Congresswoman] Sewell, too.”

But Republicans’ plan to isolate Figures and move the state one step closer to an all-Republican congressional delegation didn’t quite work. 

Figures moved to Montgomery and mounted an aggressive campaign to retain his seat—a campaign focused on affordability, agriculture and improving rural access to health care. It would be a winning combination. 

A Blue Win in Deep Red Alabama

Figures said unlike some national pundits, he wasn’t surprised by the election results. 

“A lot of these national race raters and experts have never spent a day in Alabama,” Figures said. “They’ve never worked a race in Alabama. They don’t even have friends or family in Alabama. They just look at numbers on a screen.”

But Figures and his team knew what was happening on the ground in the district for one simple reason: They were actually there, listening to voters.

“They’re tired of the breakdown in decency. Tired of the breakdown in norms. Tired of being lied to by the government, particularly by the White House. ‘I’m going to lower prices on day one.’ Did not happen. ‘I’m not getting into forever wars.’ Did not happen. ‘I’m going to release the Epstein Files.’ Did not happen.”

Another clear factor? 

“Gas prices, gas prices, gas prices,” Figures said. “And they’re high right now because of an optional war that we are in in Iran.”

The war has also impacted farmers in Figures’ district as fertilizer prices spike as a result of shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. 

Eckelman, the Montevallo political science professor, said that some of the fragile coalitions that provided the GOP such decisive victories in the past have also begun to erode, even in places in Alabama considered deep Trump country. And while Alabama didn’t see Democrats take any major offices statewide, Eckelman said that victories like Figures’ will serve as examples of what a winning Democratic campaign in a Republican state could look like. 

“The national media and the national Democratic Party may not pay much attention to Alabama, but things are happening here,” Eckelman said. The state’s Democratic Party infrastructure, for example, is improving for the first time in decades, and the party is able to recruit better candidates up and down the ticket, she said. 

Former U.S. Sen. Doug Jones was the party’s nominee for governor, coming within four points of Sen. Tommy Tuberville, a Republican and former Auburn football coach, in the race for governor, the closest margin for the office in decades. Figures called Alabama’s gubernatorial race the largest swing to the left in the country, despite the outcome. 

Down the line, Figures and Sewell may have to deal with efforts to again redraw district lines to oust them from congress. But for now, said David A. Hughes, a political scientist at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette who studies Alabama politics, progressives in the state can rest assured that Democrats in Alabama did better on Nov. 3 than they have in years.

“Go look at the election map of Alabama,” Hughes said. “All 67 counties shifted toward the Democratic side compared to the last election. That’s saying something.”

Figures agreed.

“There’s hope,” he said. “There’s a lot of work to be done, but we’ve made significant strides. And I do think there’s more on the horizon.”

news.title: Republicans Won Fewer Than Half of Trump’s Gen Z Voters in Midterms—Poll
news.text: Fewer than half of Gen Z voters who cast their ballots for President Donald Trump in the 2024 election backed Republicans in the 2026 midterm elections, according to a new J.L. Partners post-midterm poll. Republicans lost more ground among Gen Z than any other age group, with only 42 percent of Gen Z voters who supported Trump heading to the polls to vote for Republican candidates this year, the poll found. While some of these voters backed Democrats this time around, the major shift was due to a collapse in turnout. Sixteen percent of Gen Z Trump voters supported Democratic candidates this year, while 34 percent did not vote, according to the poll. It surveyed 1,000 registered voters on Election Day and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points. The new data come as Republicans continue to grapple with difficult midterm election results. Democrats won comfortable majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate in an environment defined by Trump’s declining national approval rating and frustration over the state of the economy and gas prices. Democrats saw gains across demographic groups, but the Gen Z shift is especially notable because young voters shifted toward Trump from 2020 to 2024, helping propel his victory over former Vice President Kamala Harris, defying their reputation as being one of the most progressive voting blocs. Two years later, Trump’s gains among the youngest voters in the country have appeared to evaporate, with the poll suggesting Republicans have struggled to replicate Trump’s success with Gen Z voters. Newsweek reached out to the Republican National Committee (RNC) for comment via email. Where Republicans Lost Votes—What Poll Shows Gen Z was the age group that saw the most significant defections from Trump in this year’s midterms, the poll found. But the poll also found that Hispanic Trump voters shifted away from the GOP. It found that only 37 percent of Hispanic Trump 2024 voters cast their ballots for Republicans this year, compared to 7 percent who supported Democrats and 46 percent who simply stayed home. Democrats did particularly well in places with a high concentration of Hispanic voters. They nearly flipped two House seats in South Florida and swept statewide races in Arizona and Nevada, two swing states that narrowly backed Trump two years earlier. But the shift was especially important in Texas, a traditionally conservative state that Democrats flipped this year. Democrats won the Senate race, governorship and several other statewide offices. They also won back voters in South Texas, a former Democratic stronghold that shifted toward Trump in 2024. In total, 52 percent of Trump’s 2024 voters cast their ballots for Republican candidates, the poll found. Eight percent voted for Democrats, while 35 percent stayed home during the midterms. How Did Gen Z Vote in 2024? Voters between the ages of 18 and 29 shifted rightward from 2020 to 2024, backing Harris by only an 11-point margin, 54 percent to 43 percent, according to CNN exit polling data. Former President Joe Biden won that age group by 24 points in 2020, while former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton won them by 19 points in 2016, exit polling data found. How Did Gen Z Vote in the Midterms? Gen Z shifted significantly leftward in the 2026 midterms, backing Democrats by 50 points, 74 percent to 24 percent, according to CNN exit polling. They backed Democrats by a larger margin than any other age group. Democrats won voters between 30 and 44 by 28 points, voters between 45 and 64 by 7 points and those 65 and older by a single point, according to exit polling data. Trump’s approval rating had fallen with all groups, but especially with Gen Z voters. Recent polling from YouGov and The Economist, conducted from November 4 to 6 among 3,166 registered voters, found that only 30 percent of 18 to 29-year-olds approved of Trump, compared to 66 percent of whom disapproved of him. Young voters comprise a modest share of the electorate—about 11 percent, according to exit polling data—but those shifts contributed to Democrats’ blue tsunami that carried them to victory across the country. Gen Z voters proved important in several key races. In the Texas Senate race, where Democratic Senator-elect James Talarico defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton by about 12 points, Gen Z backed Talarico by 60 points, 79 percent to 19 percent, according to exit polls. Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed won voters between 18 and 29 by a 41-point margin against Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s Senate race, 69 percent to 28 percent, helping contribute to his 7-point statewide win. Meanwhile, Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, won 18-29 voters by 72 points, 85 percent to 13 percent, over Republican Mike Collins in his reelection bid. Only 9 percent of voters between the ages of 18 and 29 considered themselves to be MAGA, while 34 percent said they would describe themselves as a democratic socialist, according to the CNN exit poll data. Forty-nine percent said they’re liberal, 31 percent described themselves as moderate, while only 20 percent said they were conservative. Dissatisfaction with Trump and the economy may have fueled Republicans’ collapse with young voters. Most of those voters—83 percent—said they disapproved of Trump, with only 17 percent saying they approved of him on Election Day. The economy was a major driving factor for Gen Z, with 93 percent describing the cost of living as being crucial or major in deciding their vote. Seventy percent also said the Iran war was crucial or major in deciding their vote, the polling found. House and Senate Election Results 2026 Nearly two weeks after the midterms, the majority of House and Senate races have been called by the Associated Press. As of Monday, Democrats were projected to hold 256 seats in the House, compared to Republicans’ 170 seats. In the Senate, the AP projected 55 seats going to Democrats with 44 seats going to Republicans. Which Races Are Still Undecided? Some races were still uncalled Monday evening. The most prominent uncalled race was the Alaska Senate contest, where Democrat Mary Peltola, a former representative, led GOP Senator Dan Sullivan by nearly 4 points—49.9 percent to 46 percent. If no candidate reaches an outright majority, the race would go to ranked choice. The following House races also remained uncalled. Furthermore, two Louisiana House races will head to a runoff, with no candidate receiving a majority. Republicans are seen as having an advantage in both races. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Republicans struggled to replicate Trump's inroads with the nation's youngest voters, a new poll found.

news.title: What a night in Chicago exposes about the end of the Trump era
news.text:
At 8:23 p.m. Central Time on Sunday, August 23, 2026, I watched a woman drop her pants and go to the bathroom on the sidewalk.

I was standing on Upper Wacker Drive in downtown Chicago, on one of those surreal, beautiful nights that looks like something a tourism board would Photoshop onto its website. A surveyor could have used her as a reference point to draw a straight line from me to Trump Tower.

I will remember that image for the rest of my life.

How do I know the exact date and time? I left myself a voice memo. “Yup. This is America right now. We have got to get out of this place.”

She wasn’t the problem.

The Trump regime and all in its orbit have deeply soiled this nation.

In beautiful prose at The Atlantic, Adam Kirsch asks a question that has become increasingly difficult to avoid: “Does Donald Trump mean anything?...Trump has certainly been transformative, so it stands to reason that there is such a thing as Trumpism. …So it’s only now, as Trumpism seems to be fading as a political force, that its true meaning can be seen clearly.”

I see the meaning in the images — images that I will never forget.

Trump descending a golden escalator in 2015 to announce his first presidential campaign.

The forlorn faces of Hillary Clinton’s and Kamala Harris’s supporters on two election nights at their respective “victory” rallies, eight years apart.

Thousands of Trump’s MAGA followers overrunning the Capitol on Jan. 6, one of them waving a Confederate battle flag.

A bloodied Trump, standing up after an assassin’s bullet nearly killed him, fist raised in the air, shouting, “Fight! Fight! Fight!”

A five-year-old child in Minneapolis carrying his Spider-Man backpack and clutching a blue bunny, being used by ICE enforcers as bait to lure out his father.

The video-recorded killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good by federal immigration agents.

President Trump delivering his final campaign rally speech on November 2, 2026, to a crowd of dozens in front of his befouled Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, with the Washington Monument seemingly staring down at him in judgment.

America needs a deep moral cleansing of its political system and political culture. Trumpism and MAGA are symptoms of a deep rot, not its cause.

To wit. Last Thursday, the Department of Homeland Security issued a press release celebrating its mass deportation terror campaign and its historic “success” in removing 483,200 “illegal aliens” from the country during the last fiscal year:

This “success” looks like an 8-year-old Haitian child wearing his best dress shirt and slacks to a hearing, only to be detained for deportation.

This “success” means unaccompanied migrant children being told they will receive $3,000 if they “self-deport.”

The nurse has been effectively disappeared, lost in a system in which ICE contractors were given scripts to help ensure that thousands of detainees cannot be found.

At least 59 people — and likely many more — have died in ICE detention. In response to concerns about safety and living conditions, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters, “We’re not providing Holiday Inns.”

A healthy society should strive for what is better, what is best, and what is just. Instead, the Trump regime — and, more importantly, the much larger corrupt leadership class that empowered the Age of Trump — are pursuing the opposite.

Does Trumpism mean anything? Former Republican strategist Steve Schmidt offers an answer, and a warning in a new video.

"When a star begins its death cycle, it collapses. But as it collapses and gets smaller, it does not get lighter or dimmer. It gets hotter. It gets brighter. It gets denser. It gets heavier. And for a political party, it gets crazier.

And so, in the end there will be on the Mar-a-Lago patio the purest and vilest and meanest distillation of MAGA. Its filthiest, rottenest, most despicable depraved remnant will gather there and there will be MAGA in its final form."

The Democrats will not take control of Congress until next January.

A blue tsunami in the midterm elections gave Democrats control of both the House and Senate, with surprise victories in deep-red states such as Texas, Georgia, and Mississippi. Trump told the American people to vote as if he was on the ballot — and they did. The tens of millions in the “coalition of the decent” have given the Democrats a mandate to clean up a dirty, broken political system.

They must investigate and hold public hearings into the administration’s corruption, self-dealing, influence-peddling, profiteering, and other crimes and abuses of the law and democratic norms.

There should also be impeachment hearings for all administration officials — not just Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth — who have violated the public trust or otherwise failed to fulfill their duties. “I was just following orders” is no defense. Of course, President Trump himself has earned a third impeachment.

The Democrats have a responsibility to confront spiraling costs for food, housing, gas, and healthcare, which have pushed more Americans into dire financial precarity while corporations and other gangster capitalists enrich themselves — a class that includes the president and his cabal.

The so-called “Big Beautiful Bill” must be dismantled.

Trump’s illegal Iran war must also be defunded. Congress has the power of the purse. They must use it.

Democrats must also resist their worst tendencies toward compromise and bipartisanship. As Ray Richmond writes at Raw Story, this means refusing to give the Republicans an olive branch that they will turn into a spear. Democrats must not confuse righteous justice with unjust retribution.

Ultimately, Democrats must make peace with — if not embrace — the fact that if they are doing their jobs correctly, their hands are going to get very dirty. De-Trumpification is going to be very nasty. Are the Democrats ready?

Do they have the stomach to do the hard work?

Chauncey DeVega is a politics and opinion writer. He was formerly a senior politics writer at Salon. His essays, commentary, interviews and other writing have been cited by The New York Times, The Washington Post, the BBC, NPR, The Atlantic and other leading publications. He hosts two podcasts, The Chauncey DeVega Show and The Truth Report.

Read an expanded version of this essay on his Substack, Indomitable.

news.title: Julian Epstein: “I Don’t Think AOC Is A Serious Candidate”
news.text:
Full Interview:

Full Transcript:

Guy Benson: Well, we’re joined now by Julian Epstein, who was chief counsel to the House Judiciary Committee and a staff director to the House Oversight Committee under the Democrats in the late 90s and early 2000s. Julian, good to have you back here.

Julian Epstein: Hey Guy, it’s a pleasure being with you always. I always tend to learn something from you watching you on Fox and in our discussion. So it’s great to be back.

Guy Benson: That’s very kind of you to say and we like having you here as well, although we kind of have to talk through what happened two weeks ago tomorrow and commiserate a bit. I know that you were very concerned about the direction of your political party. Some of the races in particular were of great interest to you. We talked a lot about Michigan, the Senate race there, and that race, like almost all of them–basically every competitive race, and then some that didn’t seem competitive then became competitive–went one direction in this washout blue wave tsunami situation. And now you’ve got a party with enormous governing majorities in Congress at least coming into play starting in January, and I think you’ve got a lot of people now jockeying for sort of positions of power into the future, whether in leadership or at the presidential level, or really trying to influence which wing or part of the party ends up on top and kind of supreme. And there’s a lot of battles playing out right now for that control, and one of the proxy fights is this Chuck Schumer majority leader question. He says he’s got the votes. I’ve seen reporting that he’s got the votes; he just needs a majority of the incoming caucus to become majority leader. We’ve got this Chris Van Hollen from Maryland who is his challenger. He says that’s nonsense and he’s going to be fighting this thing out. He, of course, has been pandering hard to the progressive wing, the left-wingers on Israel. He’s turned sharply against Israel. He’s gone to bat for criminal illegal immigrants. He’s kind of gone, you know, face-first in the tank for the whole left-wing agenda. So that’s one of these battles that’s already brewing. How do you read it? And if in fact you do believe that Schumer’s fine, he’ll be fine and be elected, what kind of leash will he have? Because I know the base, right? The base reviles him.

Julian Epstein: Yeah, I think that’s the right question, Guy, and thanks again for having me on. I think the news media is missing what’s going on here. They’re treating this as a horse race, and it’s not a horse race–it’s a flex. It’s a flex by the progressives and the socialists in the party, and Schumer does have the votes. He’s probably got 29, which is the amount of votes that he needs.

Guy Benson: Some of the numbers have it higher and into like the upper 30s even, so we’ll see.

Julian Epstein: Yeah, what Van Hollen is trying to do on behalf of the socialists and the hard leftists is to tell Schumer that the caucus is divided and that if he wants to get anything done, Schumer is going to have to capitulate. He’s going to have to make major concessions to the hard left. Now, what those concessions are is yet to be determined. You’ve got people like Ron Wyden, who’s talking about spending $8 or $10 million–$8 to $10 trillion–on new tax-and-spend welfare spending. You’ve got a big portion of the Democratic caucus that wants to isolate Israel and take away its ability for self-defense in what is a war against fascism in the Middle East. You’ve sort of got the Green New Deal agenda that’s trying to be revived by the socialists. It’s not clear what exactly Van Hollen would do on behalf of the socialists and the hard left, but what he’s saying is, “I’ve got a group of 15, 20 senators who, if you want to get anything done, you’re going to have to capitulate to them.” And that’s what this is about.

Guy Benson: Medicare for All also being, you know, one of these demands you’re seeing creeping up on the left.

Julian Epstein: I tell you, that’s a con job. I don’t even think they’re going to bring Medicare for All up for a vote, because they tried to do this, I think it was 2019. And as soon as voters realize that it’s going to mean an end to their employer-based insurance and substitute it for a very lousy form of government-run insurance, the numbers turn immediately. They go, let’s say, 80-20 against it. And the Democrats know that this whole Medicare for All campaign slogan was a complete con job. I would bet a dollar to a donut that it never comes up for a vote.

Guy Benson: I think it may not come up for a vote in the upcoming Congress. I think they want to keep the idea alive, get the trifecta, and then do a lot of things if they can, including Medicare for All, but that’s–

Julian Epstein: Well, it’s grandstanding. It’s grandstanding, this demagoguery. They hope that the public doesn’t look at this the way they hope the public doesn’t look at the rest of what’s going on. I mean, the federal government is functionally insolvent right now. We’re $40 trillion in debt with $2 trillion every year adding on to that. We, you know, we are going in the direction of France very, very slowly, but surely. And you know, you look at the con job that’s being told by a welfare state that continues to fail. Obamacare was supposed to solve the problem for the uninsured and the underinsured, right? And what Obamacare has done is it’s killed competition, it’s increased consolidation, and it’s basically been a blank check for insurance companies.

Guy Benson: Well, and premiums keep going up. I saw there was like a double-digit premium increase this year under the quote-unquote Affordable Care Act, which is the last time Democrats–

Julian Epstein: They’re expecting 14%–I think the number is somewhere between 12 and 14%. But it stands to reason that this would happen, because basically what the federal government is saying to insurance companies is, “Charge whatever you like for the most part, and the consumer, the patient is only going to have to pay a small fraction of those costs, and the government will pay the rest.” And so it’s a blank check for insurance companies. And it was very foreseeable. Conservatives pointed that out at the time, but not loudly enough. I mean, the conservative message machine here during the midterms and even now is just horrible.

Guy Benson: I mean, I do think, in fairness, I do think conservatives won the argument on Obamacare and won huge majorities to try to stop it in 2010. But it was too late. Democrats jammed it through anyway. And I think they would love to do the same with a government takeover of health care if they have the votes–probably not again in the next two years, but thereafter, if they had all of those levers of power. But I just want to come back, because the Van Hollen thing, you’re calling it a flex. I started to identify him as someone with clear national ambitions the moment he started really turning on Israel, because that’s kind of the spirit of the base of the party right now, where you cannot go anywhere in national Democratic politics unless you are foaming at the mouth about the Jewish state. And then, you know, his stunt going down and having whatever the margaritas with the criminal alien, all of that. He is pandering to that very sizable base. They feel emboldened, and I know that the more moderate folks are saying, “Look, without us, we don’t have these big majorities.” I don’t think that the left-wingers care. I think the left-wingers are like, “We’ve got these majorities. We’ve shown that we can win even in a place like Michigan, and now we’ve got to govern like left-wing socialists, and if you’re not going to do it, you’re going to have big, big problems.” I feel like the Dems are going to have lots of wiggle room, right? Margin for error given the size of these majorities, but there are some underlying tensions that could bubble to the surface, especially in an upcoming presidential primary where you’re going to have a lot of people running that hard-left route to try to get to the White House and saying, “Listen, we can win. It doesn’t matter what we believe in, what we say. 2026 proves that this stuff can win nationwide.” And are they wrong?

Julian Epstein: Yeah, they’re wrong. And they’re wrong. I mean, the Democratic Party, Guy, continues to be 10 points behind the Republican Party in terms of public favorability and brand favorability.

Guy Benson: Yeah, they just won 56 Senate seats and 260 House seats, though.

Julian Epstein: That’s not because anything they’re doing is popular. That’s because people were repulsed by what Trump is doing, which is he is spending too much time on vanity projects and not enough time on a plan for the future. And he was god-awful in terms of explaining what was a very noble undertaking in Iran. This is something that has to be explained to the public, which wasn’t, except for these one-offs. And it was a rejection of Trump. It was not any kind of mandate or validation of what the Democrats were arguing. The Democrats continue to be far, far, far to the left of the median voter, much further left than the Republicans are to the right of the median. The Republicans align with the median voters much better than Democrats do, but you know, when we have more time, I could just go through the number of just dismal communications failures and strategic failures on the part of the Republican Party. I mean, the Republican Party was sort of right. I think that Trump was right on the economic plan in terms of deregulation and tax cuts. Look at the economy. We’re at 3.4 GDP growth. He was right on Iran. He is right on closed borders. But these things were poorly executed and poorly communicated. I wanted him to succeed on all these things because I think they were right, and I think also undermined–

Guy Benson: And also undermined by some other stuff as well, so like that’s–well, undermined by JD Vance, for sure.

Julian Epstein: Look, the worst mistake that this administration made was the pause on October 7th–I’m sorry, on April 7th–of the war, because we were, I think, a month away from finishing the job, and I think the administration was duped when Iran said, “Let’s talk,” and I think Qatar and Pakistan played a role in duping the administration, and so that was a disaster. That’s one issue, but let’s return back to what you were asking about Van Hollen. There’s one point that you missed about Van Hollen in terms of his flex, and the socialist agenda is all the flex. I don’t think any of it is a serious set of policy ideas that could ever pass or bring meaningful change. But the one idea that you missed was he wants to raise–he’s talking about raising the marginal tax rate to 50% at the federal level. Okay, when you put that together with state and local taxes, you’re talking about for the most productive amongst us, the job creators, you’re talking about a tax rate of 70% when you include state and local. That means that if you are the most productive, if you are a job creator, if you are an innovator, you are going to have to effectively work for the government between January and October. Right? You get two or three months out of the year where you’re actually making income that goes to yourself rather than the federal government.

Guy Benson: But Julian, a lot of people in your party would say that’s just a fair share and they can afford it. That’s the mantra.

Julian Epstein: Yeah. Well, I don’t think many of them understand economics. If you look at the people in the party saying that, none of them have ever spent any time in the private sector building, innovating, discovering anything. I agree, but like if they’ve got the–

Guy Benson: Power, they’re going to do it. This is what is…

Julian Epstein: Well, look at what happened. I mean, again, to the point about the Democrats not having a mandate, look what happened in California, look what happened with these wealth taxes. And one of the things that the Republican Party is not explaining–they’re very much on the defensive on this “tax the rich”–is, you know, if you’re a billionaire, right? And you’re making X amount in passive and active income, a tiny, tiny fraction of that income that you’re getting is being spent on your own personal consumption, whatever luxury you may have. A tiny fraction–90 to 95% of that is the money that goes back into the investment economy. The economy that’s going to provide the AI revolution, the economy that has to invest in our factories and providing new jobs. That is the engine of our economic growth. So, when they’re talking about taking 70% of what they earn and taking it from the productive investment economy and putting it into the unproductive welfare state economy, you’re talking about, again, going back in the direction of France that has less than 1%–

Guy Benson: No, I agree, Julian. I don’t disagree with anything that you’re saying. I just worry.

Julian Epstein: My point is not that you and I disagree, Guy; my point is that there is nobody out there on the Republican side making this argument in an effective way. You know, Milton Friedman used to make this argument on behalf of Ronald Reagan, and it was extremely effective. And it was extremely persuasive, including–even though they didn’t want to admit it–with liberals, moderate liberals in that time. This argument is not being joined in a meaningful way by people that oppose it. And that is why it’s gaining currency amongst particularly a Gen Z population that is looking for easy answers, that does not study, that doesn’t have any depth of understanding, and that is frankly in many cases a lazy generation. And until people start countering this nonsense with reality, it’s going to continue.

Guy Benson: Now you’ve got to address the real frustrations, which do exist, but you’ve got to do it on substance with ideas that work. That’s not, I think, what we’ve seen, especially in this cycle, which brings us again, looking ahead. We talked about sort of this skirmish over Senate leadership; I think that’s small potatoes compared to the presidential race. I was on TV earlier today. I think there’s this report out that the DSA chapter in New York is urging AOC to run for president. I think she is strongly considering it. And I think that she could get the nomination. I’m not saying she’s destined to get it, but if it’s seen as Bernie Sanders handing her the torch and it’s a very crowded field and she’s got a lot of energy and, you know, young leftists behind her, I could see a path to the nomination. And if the electorate is in a mood two years from now like they were two weeks ago, I think she could win a general election. Do you disagree?

Julian Epstein: I completely disagree. First of all, just circling back to my point about the DSA and the conservative communications machine. I mean, every time you talk about the DSA endorsing somebody, one of the first things that opponents should be out there saying, which I’ve said, is that the DSA is an organization that supports fascism. The DSA cheered for the October 7th massacre, which is based on an ideology that goes directly back to Nazi Germany. The 1988 Hamas Charter is a direct descendant of Mein Kampf, and nobody makes that argument. If this was an organization that was supporting a genocide against Black or brown folks, every time they did anything, it’s the first thing the left would remind you of, and yet the right and moderates don’t say anything.

Guy Benson: And they’re also super radical on policing and prisons and all. I mean, you go down the list, their entire agenda is crazy.

Julian Epstein: Yeah, look at Mamdani with the response to the special response unit in New York. No question. But I think more importantly with AOC is I don’t think AOC is a very serious candidate. I don’t think she has a great deal of depth or substance, and there’s plenty of examples of that. When she was asked about strategic ambiguity in Taiwan, she had no clue what that was. When she was asked a couple years ago on a show called Firing Line about the situation in Gaza and the West Bank, she fumbled her way through. It was clear she didn’t even have a freshman college student’s understanding of the issue. She was a bartender before she was a member of Congress. And any time she’s in a situation where she’s asked on serious policy issues to explain something, she sort of, you know, lapses into a Kamala Harris evasion or stream of consciousness or something that is other than, you know, deep-think substance. So I think she is an influencer. I mean, that’s the unfortunate thing about what’s happening in our politics is we have entered into an influencer era where–

Guy Benson: I agree, which is why I think, Julian, we could have an influencer election if we haven’t already had one, and if the political mood is aligned a certain way, I think a very substanceless, destructive-ideology-type candidate could win.
